entries.meaning: To come up or come into being — of problems, questions, and opportunities; in formal or older use, to get up.
examples: Questions arise every time the budget changes midyear.
A dispute arose over who owned the fence.
New evidence has arisen since the trial began.
If the need arises, call me at home.
Most complaints arise from a single billing error.
The lawsuit arose out of a contract signed in 1998.
Several claims have arisen from the same accident.
The congregation arises for the final hymn.
He arose before dawn and made coffee in the dark.
She had arisen early every day of that long summer.

senses.head: Come up, occur (of a situation)
body: The everyday sense: questions, problems, needs, and opportunities arise. It never takes an object — you raise a question, but a question arises. (возникать, появляться)
examples: Questions arise every time the budget changes midyear.
A dispute arose over who owned the fence.
New evidence has arisen since the trial began.
If the need arises, call me at home.

senses.head: Arise from, arise out of
body: With from or out of: to have something as its cause or origin. Standard in formal, legal, and academic writing. (проистекать, быть следствием)
examples: Most complaints arise from a single billing error.
The lawsuit arose out of a contract signed in 1998.
Several claims have arisen from the same accident.

senses.head: Get up, rise (formal)
body: Literary and elevated — standing up, or getting out of bed. Ordinary American speech uses get up. (вставать, подниматься)
examples: The congregation arises for the final hymn.
He arose before dawn and made coffee in the dark.
She had arisen early every day of that long summer.

entries.register: neutral to formal — ordinary in writing, less common in speech
entries.contrast: Arise takes no object: situations arise, but you raise a question and a person rises from a chair. It follows rise exactly, and the same trap applies — the past arose cannot do participle duty: not a problem has arose but a problem has arisen.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, but with an abstract subject: problems, questions, and needs arise. No linking or stative use.
entries.transitivity: intransitive only, in every sense — a dispute arose, claims arise from the accident. You raise a question; ✗ he arose the issue.
entries.passive: no — there is no object to promote: ✗ a dispute was arisen over the fence. Only the active a dispute arose is possible.

entries.meaning: To happen to someone, nearly always something unwelcome.
examples: Whatever troubles befall us, we handle them together.
A string of disasters befell the company that winter.
Nothing like this has befallen the town in living memory.
He wondered what had befallen the crew of the second boat.
Misfortune befalls the careless traveler.
It befell on the third night that the gate stood open.
Strange things have befallen since the comet passed.

senses.head: Happen to someone (something bad)
body: Formal and literary. Unlike plain fall it takes a person or a place as its object, and what befalls is misfortune — trouble, disaster, harm. (случаться с кем-л., приключаться)
examples: Whatever troubles befall us, we handle them together.
A string of disasters befell the company that winter.
Nothing like this has befallen the town in living memory.
He wondered what had befallen the crew of the second boat.
Misfortune befalls the careless traveler.

senses.head: Come to pass (archaic)
body: The older objectless use, meaning simply to happen. Found in scripture and folktale, not in current American speech. (происходить, статься)
examples: It befell on the third night that the gate stood open.
Strange things have befallen since the comet passed.

entries.register: formal — literary and journalistic; ordinary speech says happened to
entries.contrast: Built on fall and inflected exactly like it. Unlike plain fall, it takes a person as its object — misfortune befell them — so not he befell down the stairs.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; the subject is an event or a misfortune, not a person who acts.
entries.transitivity: transitive in the living sense, with a person or place as the object — a string of disasters befell the company. The archaic sense 2 is intransitive: it befell on the third night.
entries.passive: no in practice — transitive but it resists promotion: ✗ the company was befallen by disasters. Keep the active, or switch to was struck by.

entries.meaning: To leave property to someone in a will, and by extension to pass anything on to those who come after you.
examples: Wealthy donors often bequeath their libraries to a university.
Her will bequeathed the house to her sister, not to her son.
The family has bequeathed three paintings to the museum since 1980.
He bequeaths nothing to anyone who contests the estate.
Each administration bequeaths its unfinished business to the next.
That century bequeathed us both the vaccine and the bomb.
Their teachers have bequeathed them a whole vocabulary for it.
The parish record says the merchant bequoth his lands to the abbey.
Scholars still argue over what the founder had bequothen to the town.

senses.head: Leave in a will
body: The legal sense, used of money and personal property. In modern American English the verb is regular: bequeathed, have bequeathed. (завещать, оставлять по завещанию)
examples: Wealthy donors often bequeath their libraries to a university.
Her will bequeathed the house to her sister, not to her son.
The family has bequeathed three paintings to the museum since 1980.
He bequeaths nothing to anyone who contests the estate.

senses.head: Hand down to later generations
body: Figurative: to leave something non-material — a legacy, a problem, a body of work — to whoever comes next. (передавать по наследству (традицию, наследие))
examples: Each administration bequeaths its unfinished business to the next.
That century bequeathed us both the vaccine and the bomb.
Their teachers have bequeathed them a whole vocabulary for it.

senses.head: Strong forms bequoth, bequothen (archaic)
body: The strong inflection listed for this verb survives only in old wills and literary imitations of them. Do not use it in anything you write today. (завещать (устаревшие формы))
examples: The parish record says the merchant bequoth his lands to the abbey.
Scholars still argue over what the founder had bequothen to the town.

entries.register: formal — wills and legacies; the strong bequoth/bequothen are archaic
entries.contrast: In modern American English bequeath is a regular verb: bequeathed, have bequeathed. The strong forms bequoth and bequothen listed here are archaic and turn up only in old wills and literary imitations of them — do not use them in anything you write today. Note the voiced ending, /bɪˈkwið/ like breathe, not like teeth.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, a verb of transfer like give.
entries.transitivity: ditransitive — that century bequeathed us the vaccine, or with to: her will bequeathed the house to her sister.
entries.passive: yes — the house was bequeathed to her sister, and three paintings have been bequeathed to the museum.

entries.meaning: To sit or stand with a leg on either side of something; figuratively, to dominate an entire field.
examples: That one company has bestridden the industry for twenty years.
A single firm now bestrides the entire market.
By 1900 the railroads had bestridden the continent.
Bronze generals bestride half the squares in Europe.
He bestrode the fallen log and pulled the rope tight.
The rider bestrode a gray mare and led the parade.
A stone causeway lets you bestride the stream without wading.
The arch bestrode the whole road until 1912.

senses.head: Dominate, tower over
body: The sense still in use, and always literary or journalistic: one firm or figure bestrides an industry or an era. (господствовать, довлеть над)
examples: That one company has bestridden the industry for twenty years.
A single firm now bestrides the entire market.
By 1900 the railroads had bestridden the continent.

senses.head: Sit or stand astride
body: The literal sense — a leg on each side of a horse, a log, or a wall. Ordinary American speech says sit astride instead. (сидеть верхом; стоять расставив ноги)
examples: Bronze generals bestride half the squares in Europe.
He bestrode the fallen log and pulled the rope tight.
The rider bestrode a gray mare and led the parade.

senses.head: Step across, span
body: Rare and old: to cross something in a single stride, or of a structure to span it. (перешагивать; перекрывать собой)
examples: A stone causeway lets you bestride the stream without wading.
The arch bestrode the whole road until 1912.

entries.русский: сидеть верхом; стоять расставив ноги; перешагивать
entries.register: rare — literary and headline use; Americans say sat astride or dominated
entries.contrast: Built on stride and inflected exactly like it, never bestrided. It is literary; in ordinary American speech you would say sat astride or dominated.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in the literal bestride a log; closer to stative in the dominating sense, where it describes a standing position rather than an act.
entries.transitivity: transitive in every sense, and the object is obligatory — one firm bestrides the market; ✗ the general bestrode for years.
entries.passive: restricted — grammatical but rare and stiff: the industry has been bestridden by one company is possible in literary writing, though the active is far more natural.

entries.meaning: To offer a price, at auction or for a contract; in an older and more formal sense, to command, to greet, or to invite.
examples: Two collectors bid against each other for the manuscript.
She bid nine hundred dollars and got the table.
Three people have bid on that lamp already.
Small contractors rarely bid on federal jobs.
They bid too low and lost money on the project.
The city had bid for the tournament twice before.
He bids his students think for themselves.
The sergeant bade them wait outside the tent.
The captain has bidden the crew to stand down.
She bade us good night and went upstairs.
We bade farewell at the gate and drove home.
They have bidden their guests welcome in three languages.
The steward bade the whole village to the wedding.
The host had bidden the guests to arrive at seven.
Only those bidden to the feast came through the gate.

senses.head: Offer a price at auction
body: In this sense the verb never changes shape: bid, bid, bid. Not he bade forty dollars. (предлагать цену (на аукционе), торговаться)
examples: Two collectors bid against each other for the manuscript.
She bid nine hundred dollars and got the table.
Three people have bid on that lamp already.

senses.head: Bid on / bid for a contract
body: Business use with on or for: to submit a formal offer to do work at a stated price. The forms stay invariant here too. (подавать заявку, участвовать в тендере)
examples: Small contractors rarely bid on federal jobs.
They bid too low and lost money on the project.
The city had bid for the tournament twice before.

senses.head: Command, tell someone to do
body: Formal and literary — this is the sense that carries the strong forms bade and bidden. It takes a bare infinitive: bid them come in. (велеть, приказывать)
examples: He bids his students think for themselves.
The sergeant bade them wait outside the tent.
The captain has bidden the crew to stand down.

senses.head: Bid farewell, bid good night
body: A fixed formula for greetings and farewells: bid someone welcome, farewell, good night. Most Americans say bade as /bæd/, rhyming with had. (прощаться; желать (доброй ночи))
examples: She bade us good night and went upstairs.
We bade farewell at the gate and drove home.
They have bidden their guests welcome in three languages.

senses.head: Invite (archaic)
body: Old use, alive today mostly in the phrase the bidden guests. Modern English uses invite. (приглашать, звать)
examples: The steward bade the whole village to the wedding.
The host had bidden the guests to arrive at seven.
Only those bidden to the feast came through the gate.

entries.register: everyday — auctions, contracts, and bid farewell; the forms bade/bidden are dated
entries.contrast: Bid splits by meaning. In the auction sense it never changes — bid, bid, bid: not he bade forty dollars but he bid forty dollars. The forms bade and bidden belong to the older sense of commanding or greeting: she bade him good night, the guests had been bidden to arrive at seven. Most Americans say bade as /bæd/, rhyming with had.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in every sense, from offering a price to commanding.
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive with a preposition in business (they bid on federal jobs), transitive with an amount (she bid nine hundred dollars), and ditransitive in the command and greeting senses (she bade us good night, he bids his students think for themselves).
entries.passive: yes, but sense by sense — that lamp has been bid on twice, the guests had been bidden to arrive at seven. The frozen bid farewell stays active: ✗ farewell was bidden to us.

entries.meaning: Of air, to move or to move something; of a person, to force air out of the mouth — plus a large family of idioms from blow up to blow it.
examples: Cold winds blow off the lake all winter.
It blew hard all night.
The wind has blown from the south since Tuesday.
Papers blow everywhere when that door opens.
The storm blew three shingles off the roof.
A gust has blown the umbrella into the pool.
She blows on her coffee to cool it.
He blew out all the candles at once.
Blow your nose before you come to the table.
The nurse asked whether he had blown into the tube yet.
Conductors blow the whistle before the doors close.
The referee blew the whistle on the play.
Someone has blown the horn three times.
Engineers plan to blow up the old bridge in March.
The transformer blew up during the storm.
The video has blown up on every platform.
Cheap bulbs blow within a month.
The rear tire blew on the interstate.
Somebody has blown the fuse again.
Do not blow your whole budget in the first week.
He blew an entire paycheck on concert tickets.
They have blown through the grant already.
Do not blow this.
He blew the interview by showing up late.
We have blown two chances at the title.
He blows off class whenever the surf is good.
She blew off the whole warning.
He has blown off three appointments this month.
Stories like this usually blow over.
The whole thing blew over in a week.
The controversy had blown over long before he got back.

senses.head: Of wind: move, be in motion
body: The core intransitive sense, with wind or a draft as the subject. (дуть (о ветре))
examples: Cold winds blow off the lake all winter.
It blew hard all night.
The wind has blown from the south since Tuesday.

senses.head: Move something with air
body: Transitive: air moves an object, usually with a particle — blow off, blow over, blow away. (сдувать, уносить (ветром))
examples: Papers blow everywhere when that door opens.
The storm blew three shingles off the roof.
A gust has blown the umbrella into the pool.

senses.head: Breathe out forcefully
body: Of a person directing breath at something. This covers the fixed blow out the candles and blow your nose. (дуть, выдыхать; сморкаться)
examples: She blows on her coffee to cool it.
He blew out all the candles at once.
Blow your nose before you come to the table.
The nurse asked whether he had blown into the tube yet.

senses.head: Sound a horn or a whistle
body: Used of wind instruments, whistles, and car horns. The related noun whistleblower comes from this sense. (трубить, дуть в свисток)
examples: Conductors blow the whistle before the doors close.
The referee blew the whistle on the play.
Someone has blown the horn three times.

senses.head: Blow up — explode; destroy
body: Both transitive and intransitive. Blow up also means to lose your temper, and, recently, for something to become suddenly popular. (взрывать(ся), взлетать на воздух)
examples: Engineers plan to blow up the old bridge in March.
The transformer blew up during the storm.
The video has blown up on every platform.

senses.head: Burn out, burst (a fuse, a tire)
body: Of something that fails suddenly under pressure or current. Works in both directions: the fuse blew, he blew the fuse. (перегорать (о пробке); лопнуть (о шине))
examples: Cheap bulbs blow within a month.
The rear tire blew on the interstate.
Somebody has blown the fuse again.

senses.head: Waste, squander (money)
body: Informal, with money or time as the object, often with on or through. (спустить, промотать (деньги))
examples: Do not blow your whole budget in the first week.
He blew an entire paycheck on concert tickets.
They have blown through the grant already.

senses.head: Blow it — ruin a chance
body: Informal. The object is an opportunity: a game, an interview, a lead. (провалить, упустить, испортить)
examples: Do not blow this.
He blew the interview by showing up late.
We have blown two chances at the title.

senses.head: Blow off — skip, brush aside
body: Informal: to skip an obligation, or to dismiss a person or a concern without taking it seriously. (забить на, продинамить; отмахнуться)
examples: He blows off class whenever the surf is good.
She blew off the whole warning.
He has blown off three appointments this month.

senses.head: Blow over — pass without consequence
body: Of a storm, a scandal, or an argument that ends without lasting damage. (утихнуть, сойти на нет)
examples: Stories like this usually blow over.
The whole thing blew over in a week.
The controversy had blown over long before he got back.

entries.register: everyday — one of the verbs an American uses without thinking
entries.contrast: The past blew is a homophone of blue. Not I blowed the fuse and not I have blew it — the participle needs have: I have blown it. In the phrasal senses (blow up, blow out, blow off) the same three forms apply.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic throughout, whether the subject is wind, a person, or a fuse.
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive of wind and of things that fail (cold winds blow, the rear tire blew), transitive when something is moved, sounded, or wasted (the storm blew three shingles off, he blew a paycheck).
entries.passive: yes in the transitive senses — the umbrella has been blown into the pool, the whistle was blown on the play. No passive of the intransitive the fuse blew.
entries.phrasal verbs: blow away · blow in · blow off · blow out · blow over · blow through · blow up

entries.meaning: To write something jointly with another person.
examples: The two friends co-write every song on the album.
She co-wrote the screenplay with her brother.
He has co-written four textbooks with the same colleague.
The report had been co-written by two agencies.
He co-writes a column with a retired judge.
They co-wrote the grant proposal in a single weekend.

senses.head: Write jointly with someone
body: Standard for songs, screenplays, books, and papers; the collaborator follows with. American style keeps the hyphen and stresses the second part. (писать, написать совместно)
examples: The two friends co-write every song on the album.
She co-wrote the screenplay with her brother.
He has co-written four textbooks with the same colleague.
The report had been co-written by two agencies.
He co-writes a column with a retired judge.
They co-wrote the grant proposal in a single weekend.

entries.register: neutral — standard in music, film, and publishing credits
entries.contrast: Built on write and inflected exactly like it. American style keeps the hyphen, and the stress falls on the second part: koh-RYTE, koh-ROHT, koh-RIT-n.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, a verb of creation.
entries.transitivity: transitive — the work is the object and the collaborator follows with: she co-wrote the screenplay with her brother. The object is normally obligatory.
entries.passive: yes, and it is the usual form in credits — the report had been co-written by two agencies.

entries.meaning: Of a rooster, to make its loud call; of a person, to boast about a win.
examples: She crows whenever her team wins.
He crowed about the promotion for a solid week.
They have crowed about that one game for years.
The roosters crow before the sun clears the ridge.
Their rooster has crowed every morning since April.
The old translation reads that the cock crew three times.
Antique printings of the ballad say the cock had crown twice before daybreak.
Babies crow when you lift them overhead.
The baby crowed and reached for the balloon.
He has crowed and giggled all morning.

senses.head: Boast, gloat
body: The everyday sense, mildly disapproving, usually crow about or crow over. Regular in modern American English: crowed, have crowed. (хвастаться, злорадствовать)
examples: She crows whenever her team wins.
He crowed about the promotion for a solid week.
They have crowed about that one game for years.

senses.head: Of a rooster: call
body: The literal sense. The strong past crew survives only in older and biblical English, and the participle crown is obsolete — use crowed today. (кукарекать, петь (о петухе))
examples: The roosters crow before the sun clears the ridge.
Their rooster has crowed every morning since April.
The old translation reads that the cock crew three times.
Antique printings of the ballad say the cock had crown twice before daybreak.

senses.head: Of a baby: squeal with delight
body: A small, affectionate use: the happy noise an infant makes. (гулить, радостно вскрикивать)
examples: Babies crow when you lift them overhead.
The baby crowed and reached for the balloon.
He has crowed and giggled all morning.

entries.register: neutral — the verb itself is ordinary and regular in American English; the strong crew is biblical and crown obsolete
entries.contrast: In American English crow is a regular verb: crowed, have crowed. The strong past crew survives only in older and biblical English (the cock crew), and the participle crown is obsolete — it is not the noun crown /kraʊn/, which is an unrelated word. Use crowed in your own writing, especially for the boasting sense.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; a verb of noise-making, both for the rooster and for the person gloating.
entries.transitivity: intransitive in all three senses; the thing boasted about follows about or over: he crowed about the promotion. ✗ he crowed his win.
entries.passive: no — intransitive, so there is nothing to promote: ✗ the promotion was crowed about is at best marginal, and ✗ the win was crowed.

entries.meaning: To perform an action or a task — and, as an auxiliary, the verb that carries tense in questions, negatives, and emphasis.
examples: We do the dishes right after dinner.
She did the whole route on foot.
He has done more than anyone asked him to.
By noon they had done half the packing.
Do you take cream?
She did not answer the second email.
Does he know about the meeting?
I do remember her name — give me a second.
He did apologize, eventually.
She does care, whatever she says.
She reads more than I do.
He said he would call, and he did.
Nobody has done more for this town than she has.
She does her hair before anyone else is awake.
They did the whole kitchen over a weekend.
The cleaners have done the upstairs already.
Two chairs will do for now.
A shorter rope did just fine.
Cold pizza has done the job before.
How did she do on the exam?
The store did badly its first year.
She has done well for herself.
This car does thirty miles to the gallon.
We did four hundred miles before dark.
They had done the whole loop by noon.
Nobody wants to do a day in that place.
He did eight years upstate.
She has done time for fraud.
The teacher made him do the essay over.
We did the bathroom over last spring.
They have done the whole website over twice.
We can do without a second car.
They did without heat for three days.
She has done without help all year.
I could do with a nap.
Nobody wants to do away with the program.
The district did away with letter grades.
They have done away with the paper form entirely.

senses.head: Perform, carry out
body: The core lexical sense, with a task, a job, or a chore as the object. Not I done it: the participle always needs have. (делать, выполнять)
examples: We do the dishes right after dinner.
She did the whole route on foot.
He has done more than anyone asked him to.
By noon they had done half the packing.

senses.head: Auxiliary in questions and negatives
body: Do carries the tense so the main verb stays in the base form. That is why did you went is wrong and did you go is right. (вспомогательный глагол (вопрос, отрицание))
examples: Do you take cream?
She did not answer the second email.
Does he know about the meeting?

senses.head: Emphatic do
body: Stressed do in an affirmative sentence insists on it against doubt or contradiction. (усилительное do (действительно, всё же))
examples: I do remember her name — give me a second.
He did apologize, eventually.
She does care, whatever she says.

senses.head: Stand in for another verb
body: Do substitutes for a verb already mentioned, especially in comparisons, short answers, and tag questions. (заменяет ранее названный глагол)
examples: She reads more than I do.
He said he would call, and he did.
Nobody has done more for this town than she has.

senses.head: Tidy, arrange, put in order
body: Do a room, do your hair, do the yard — to put something into the state it is supposed to be in. (приводить в порядок, убирать; делать (причёску))
examples: She does her hair before anyone else is awake.
They did the whole kitchen over a weekend.
The cleaners have done the upstairs already.

senses.head: Be enough, suffice
body: Intransitive, usually with will or would: that will do, it will do for now. (годиться, подойти, хватить)
examples: Two chairs will do for now.
A shorter rope did just fine.
Cold pizza has done the job before.

senses.head: Fare, get along
body: Always with an adverb — doing well, doing badly, how are you doing. Standard in talk about health and business alike. (поживать, справляться)
examples: How did she do on the exam?
The store did badly its first year.
She has done well for herself.

senses.head: Cover a distance or a speed
body: With a measurement as the object: miles covered, miles per gallon, speed on the highway. (проходить, проезжать (расстояние); ехать со скоростью)
examples: This car does thirty miles to the gallon.
We did four hundred miles before dark.
They had done the whole loop by noon.

senses.head: Serve a prison sentence
body: Informal but widespread: do time, do five years. (отсидеть (срок))
examples: Nobody wants to do a day in that place.
He did eight years upstate.
She has done time for fraud.

senses.head: Do over — redo from the start
body: American English keeps do over where British English says do again; a do-over is also a noun. (переделать заново)
examples: The teacher made him do the essay over.
We did the bathroom over last spring.
They have done the whole website over twice.

senses.head: Do without / could do with
body: Do without means to manage in the absence of something; could do with means to need or want it. (обходиться без; не помешало бы)
examples: We can do without a second car.
They did without heat for three days.
She has done without help all year.
I could do with a nap.

senses.head: Do away with — abolish
body: To get rid of a rule, a practice, or an institution for good. (покончить с, отменить)
examples: Nobody wants to do away with the program.
The district did away with letter grades.
They have done away with the paper form entirely.

entries.register: everyday — one of the verbs an American uses without thinking
entries.third person: does /dʌz/ (irregular in both spelling and sound) · -ing form: doing
entries.contrast: Not I done it: done always needs have, so use I did it or I have done it. As an auxiliary, do carries the tense for the main verb, which is why did you went is wrong and did you go is right. The third person is spelled does and said /dʌz/, never /duz/.
entries.verb type: both lexical and auxiliary — an action verb in do the dishes, and the tense-carrying auxiliary of questions, negatives, and emphasis (do you take cream?, I do remember), plus a pro-verb standing in for an earlier verb (she reads more than I do).
entries.transitivity: both — transitive in the lexical senses (do the dishes, do thirty miles to the gallon), intransitive in that will do and she has done well. The auxiliary takes no object at all.
entries.passive: yes in the lexical transitive senses — the upstairs has been done already, the essay had to be done over. The auxiliary and pro-verb uses have no passive: ✗ cream is done taken by you.
entries.phrasal verbs: do away with · do for · do in · do out of · do over · do up · do with · do without

entries.meaning: To make a picture with lines; to pull; and, by extension, to attract, to take out, and to end level.
examples: Architects still draw by hand for the first sketches.
She drew a map on the back of the receipt.
He has drawn the same barn a hundred times.
Two horses draw the wagon up the hill.
He drew the chair closer to the fire.
The curtains had been drawn before we arrived.
Free food draws a crowd every time.
Her first novel drew attention from three publishers.
The exhibit has drawn record crowds.
You can draw cash at any branch.
He drew a card from the top of the deck.
She has drawn her salary from the same account for years.
Do not draw conclusions from one bad week.
The report drew a sharp comparison with 2008.
Critics have drawn the obvious parallel.
A nurse will draw blood before the appointment.
He drew a long breath and started over.
They have drawn blood twice this week.
The two grandmasters usually draw when they meet.
United drew with City on Saturday.
They have drawn three matches in a row.
We should draw up a list before we shop.
The lawyer drew up the contract overnight.
The committee has drawn up new rules.
Good teachers draw on their own mistakes.
The novel drew heavily on her childhood.
He has drawn on that fund twice.
Do not draw the meeting out.
She drew him out with a few easy questions.
The negotiations have been drawn out for months.
Winter draws near.
The year drew to a close without a deal.
The season has drawn to a close.

senses.head: Make a picture, sketch
body: The most common sense, of lines made by hand rather than paint or color. (рисовать, чертить)
examples: Architects still draw by hand for the first sketches.
She drew a map on the back of the receipt.
He has drawn the same barn a hundred times.

senses.head: Pull, drag
body: Somewhat formal for plain pulling, but ordinary in fixed uses: draw the curtains, draw a chair up, horses draw a wagon. (тянуть, тащить, волочить)
examples: Two horses draw the wagon up the hill.
He drew the chair closer to the fire.
The curtains had been drawn before we arrived.

senses.head: Attract
body: Of crowds, attention, criticism, or interest — what the subject pulls toward itself. (привлекать, притягивать)
examples: Free food draws a crowd every time.
Her first novel drew attention from three publishers.
The exhibit has drawn record crowds.

senses.head: Take out, withdraw
body: Of money from an account, a card from a deck, a weapon from a holster, or water from a well. (снимать (деньги); вытаскивать, доставать)
examples: You can draw cash at any branch.
He drew a card from the top of the deck.
She has drawn her salary from the same account for years.

senses.head: Draw a conclusion, a comparison, a line
body: A fixed set of abstract objects: conclusions, distinctions, parallels, and the line you will not cross. (делать (вывод); проводить (сравнение, черту))
examples: Do not draw conclusions from one bad week.
The report drew a sharp comparison with 2008.
Critics have drawn the obvious parallel.

senses.head: Draw blood, draw a breath
body: Two set collocations: taking blood for a test or a wound, and taking in air. (брать кровь; вдохнуть)
examples: A nurse will draw blood before the appointment.
He drew a long breath and started over.
They have drawn blood twice this week.

senses.head: End level, tie (sports, chess)
body: Standard in soccer and chess; in most American sports the ordinary verb is tie, though the noun a draw is used everywhere. (сыграть вничью)
examples: The two grandmasters usually draw when they meet.
United drew with City on Saturday.
They have drawn three matches in a row.

senses.head: Draw up — compose a document
body: Of contracts, wills, plans, and lists put together in written form. (составить (документ, план, список))
examples: We should draw up a list before we shop.
The lawyer drew up the contract overnight.
The committee has drawn up new rules.

senses.head: Draw on / draw upon — use as a resource
body: To take material, money, or experience from a source you already have. (черпать, использовать (опыт, средства))
examples: Good teachers draw on their own mistakes.
The novel drew heavily on her childhood.
He has drawn on that fund twice.

senses.head: Draw out — prolong; get someone talking
body: Two related uses: making something last too long, and coaxing a quiet person into conversation. (затягивать; разговорить)
examples: Do not draw the meeting out.
She drew him out with a few easy questions.
The negotiations have been drawn out for months.

senses.head: Draw near, draw to a close
body: Of time approaching. Slightly formal, common in writing and speeches. (приближаться; подходить к концу)
examples: Winter draws near.
The year drew to a close without a deal.
The season has drawn to a close.

entries.register: everyday — one of the verbs an American uses without thinking
entries.contrast: The past drew /dru/ rhymes with do and true, not with draw; the participle is drawn, never drawed. Drawn doubles as an adjective for a tired face: she looked drawn.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in every sense, from making lines to attracting a crowd.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive in most senses (she drew a map, free food draws a crowd, you can draw cash), intransitive in architects still draw by hand, in the sports United drew with City, and in winter draws near.
entries.passive: yes in the transitive senses — the curtains had been drawn, the exhibit's crowds were drawn by the reviews, new rules have been drawn up. No passive of winter draws near.
entries.phrasal verbs: draw back · draw down · draw in · draw on · draw on, draw upon · draw out · draw up

entries.meaning: To operate a vehicle; to force someone or something into a state; and to power, push, or propel.
examples: I drive to the coast every August.
He drove nine hours without stopping.
She has driven that truck since college.
I can drive you to the airport.
My neighbor drove us home after the game.
He has driven her to every appointment.
The noise drives me crazy.
Debt drove him to sell the shop.
High rents have driven young families out of the city.
A small motor drives the belt.
Steam drove the first looms.
The pumps have been driven by solar panels since June.
Curiosity drives most of her work.
Fear drove the whole campaign.
Cheap credit has driven the boom.
Drive the stake in at an angle.
He drove the last nail at sunset.
They have driven posts along the whole fence line.
Ranchers still drive cattle to summer pasture.
The crew drove the herd across the shallow ford.
Cowboys had driven the steers north for weeks.
He can drive a ball three hundred yards.
She drove a single into right field.
He has driven in four runs tonight.
What are you driving at?
I could not tell what he was driving at.
Nobody knew what she had been driving at until later.

senses.head: Operate a vehicle
body: The core sense, transitive or intransitive. Not I have drove — the participle is driven. (водить машину, ехать за рулём)
examples: I drive to the coast every August.
He drove nine hours without stopping.
She has driven that truck since college.

senses.head: Take someone somewhere by car
body: With a person as the object: you drive them, and the destination follows. (подвозить, отвозить)
examples: I can drive you to the airport.
My neighbor drove us home after the game.
He has driven her to every appointment.

senses.head: Force into a state or an action
body: Drive someone crazy, drive prices up, drive families out — the subject pushes the object into a condition it did not choose. (доводить до, вынуждать)
examples: The noise drives me crazy.
Debt drove him to sell the shop.
High rents have driven young families out of the city.

senses.head: Power, propel (a machine)
body: Of the energy source behind machinery. Often passive: the pump is driven by a small motor. (приводить в движение, питать)
examples: A small motor drives the belt.
Steam drove the first looms.
The pumps have been driven by solar panels since June.

senses.head: Motivate, be the force behind
body: With an abstract subject — curiosity, fear, cheap credit. The participle is a common adjective for an ambitious person: a driven student. (двигать, быть движущей силой)
examples: Curiosity drives most of her work.
Fear drove the whole campaign.
Cheap credit has driven the boom.

senses.head: Hammer in, force in
body: Of nails, stakes, posts, and screws forced into place by repeated blows. (вбивать, забивать (гвоздь, кол))
examples: Drive the stake in at an angle.
He drove the last nail at sunset.
They have driven posts along the whole fence line.

senses.head: Herd animals
body: The old sense that gives us cattle drive and drover. (гнать (скот))
examples: Ranchers still drive cattle to summer pasture.
The crew drove the herd across the shallow ford.
Cowboys had driven the steers north for weeks.

senses.head: Hit hard (golf, baseball)
body: Sports use: a long, hard hit. Drive in a run is standard baseball, and the noun RBI comes from it. (сильно бить (по мячу))
examples: He can drive a ball three hundred yards.
She drove a single into right field.
He has driven in four runs tonight.

senses.head: Drive at — mean, be getting at
body: Almost always in the progressive and almost always in a question about what someone really means. (клонить к, иметь в виду)
examples: What are you driving at?
I could not tell what he was driving at.
Nobody knew what she had been driving at until later.

entries.register: everyday — one of the verbs an American uses without thinking
entries.contrast: Not I have drove — the participle is driven. Drove is also a noun (a drove of cattle), and driven works as an adjective for an ambitious person: a driven student.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; the subject is either an operator or a force.
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive in he drove nine hours, transitive with a vehicle, a person, a nail, or a herd (drive the stake in, I can drive you to the airport), and with an object plus a resultant complement in the noise drives me crazy.
entries.passive: yes — the pumps have been driven by solar panels since June, young families have been driven out of the city. No passive of the intransitive he drove nine hours.
entries.phrasal verbs: drive at · drive away · drive down · drive home · drive off · drive out · drive up

entries.meaning: To take food into the mouth and swallow it; also, to wear away, and the base of several everyday idioms.
examples: We eat dinner around seven.
He ate two bowls of chili and asked for more.
The kids have eaten already.
By the time I sat down, they had eaten every roll.
We eat out twice a week.
They ate in every night that month.
She has eaten lunch at her desk since March.
Rent eats up half her paycheck.
The delay ate up the whole morning.
Legal fees have eaten up the settlement.
Salt eats into the underside of the car.
The river ate away four feet of bank.
Rust has eaten through the pan.
Something is eating him and he will not say what.
What ate at her all week was the silence.
Guilt has eaten at him since the trial.
He had to eat his words by Friday.
She ate her words on live television.
They have eaten those words more than once.

senses.head: Consume food
body: The core sense, transitive or intransitive. The participle never stands alone: not I eaten already but I have eaten already. (есть, кушать)
examples: We eat dinner around seven.
He ate two bowls of chili and asked for more.
The kids have eaten already.
By the time I sat down, they had eaten every roll.

senses.head: Eat out / eat in — take a meal
body: Eat out means at a restaurant, eat in means at home. Both are fixed and cannot be reversed. (питаться (в ресторане или дома))
examples: We eat out twice a week.
They ate in every night that month.
She has eaten lunch at her desk since March.

senses.head: Eat up — consume entirely
body: Literal with food, and very common with time and money as the object. (съедать, поглощать (время, деньги))
examples: Rent eats up half her paycheck.
The delay ate up the whole morning.
Legal fees have eaten up the settlement.

senses.head: Eat into, eat away — corrode
body: Of acid, rust, salt, or water gradually destroying a surface, and of costs gradually destroying a margin. (разъедать, подтачивать)
examples: Salt eats into the underside of the car.
The river ate away four feet of bank.
Rust has eaten through the pan.

senses.head: Bother, trouble (what is eating you)
body: Informal, usually progressive or with at: something is quietly bothering a person. (мучить, донимать, грызть)
examples: Something is eating him and he will not say what.
What ate at her all week was the silence.
Guilt has eaten at him since the trial.

senses.head: Eat one's words
body: A fixed phrase: to be forced to admit that what you said confidently was wrong. (взять свои слова обратно)
examples: He had to eat his words by Friday.
She ate her words on live television.
They have eaten those words more than once.

entries.register: everyday — one of the verbs an American uses without thinking
entries.contrast: Americans say ate as /eɪt/, rhyming with late; the British /ɛt/ sounds out of place here. The participle never stands alone: not I eaten already but I have eaten already.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, including the figurative rust ate through the pan.
entries.transitivity: both, with an optional object — we eat dinner around seven and plain the kids have eaten already are equally good. Transitive in rent eats up half her paycheck.
entries.passive: yes where there is an object — every roll had been eaten by the time I sat down, the settlement has been eaten up by legal fees. No passive of they ate out.
entries.phrasal verbs: eat away at · eat in · eat into · eat out · eat up

entries.meaning: To drop toward the ground; to decrease; to pass into a state; and, of cities and governments, to be defeated.
examples: Leaves fall early up in the mountains.
He fell off the ladder and broke his wrist.
Snow had fallen all night on the pass.
The old barn has fallen in on itself.
Prices fall after the holidays.
The temperature fell twenty degrees in an hour.
Enrollment has fallen for three straight years.
She falls asleep on every flight.
He fell in love with the town on the first visit.
Half the crew has fallen ill.
Cities like that rarely fall without a siege.
The capital fell in three days.
The government had fallen before the vote was counted.
Soldiers fall and towns forget them.
Thousands fell on that ridge.
Men have fallen here in two wars.
Thanksgiving falls late this year.
My birthday fell on a Monday.
The deadline has fallen on a holiday twice now.
Cheap furniture falls apart in a year.
The deal fell apart over money.
He has fallen apart since the diagnosis.
Try not to fall behind on the reading.
They fell behind on the rent in March.
She has fallen behind two chapters.
Plans like that often fall through.
The sale fell through at the last minute.
Two offers have fallen through already.
People still fall for that email.
He fell for the oldest trick in the book.
I have fallen for worse scams.
It helps to have savings to fall back on.
She fell back on her old job.
They have fallen back on the same excuse all year.

senses.head: Drop toward the ground
body: The core sense, and it never takes an object: not he fell the glass but he dropped the glass. (падать)
examples: Leaves fall early up in the mountains.
He fell off the ladder and broke his wrist.
Snow had fallen all night on the pass.
The old barn has fallen in on itself.

senses.head: Decrease, go down
body: Of prices, temperatures, numbers, and rates. The opposite is rise, not raise. (падать, снижаться (о цене, температуре))
examples: Prices fall after the holidays.
The temperature fell twenty degrees in an hour.
Enrollment has fallen for three straight years.

senses.head: Pass into a state — fall asleep, fall ill
body: A fixed pattern with a short list of complements: asleep, ill, silent, in love, behind on payments. (впадать в состояние: заснуть, заболеть, влюбиться)
examples: She falls asleep on every flight.
He fell in love with the town on the first visit.
Half the crew has fallen ill.

senses.head: Be captured or defeated
body: Of cities, fortresses, and governments that lose power or are taken by an enemy. (пасть, быть захваченным (о городе, режиме))
examples: Cities like that rarely fall without a siege.
The capital fell in three days.
The government had fallen before the vote was counted.

senses.head: Die in battle
body: Formal and commemorative. The fallen is the standard collective noun for soldiers killed in war. (погибнуть (в бою))
examples: Soldiers fall and towns forget them.
Thousands fell on that ridge.
Men have fallen here in two wars.

senses.head: Occur on a date
body: Of holidays, deadlines, and anniversaries landing on a particular day. (приходиться на (дату, день недели))
examples: Thanksgiving falls late this year.
My birthday fell on a Monday.
The deadline has fallen on a holiday twice now.

senses.head: Fall apart — break down, collapse
body: Literal for objects, figurative for deals, plans, and people who stop coping. (разваливаться, рассыпаться; сорваться)
examples: Cheap furniture falls apart in a year.
The deal fell apart over money.
He has fallen apart since the diagnosis.

senses.head: Fall behind — lag
body: With on or with: to be later or further back than you should be, often about work or payments. (отставать (в учёбе, в платежах))
examples: Try not to fall behind on the reading.
They fell behind on the rent in March.
She has fallen behind two chapters.

senses.head: Fall through — fail to happen
body: Of an arrangement that collapses before it is completed. (сорваться, провалиться (о плане, сделке))
examples: Plans like that often fall through.
The sale fell through at the last minute.
Two offers have fallen through already.

senses.head: Fall for — be taken in by
body: Informal: to be fooled by a trick or a lie you should have seen through. (попасться на, повестись на)
examples: People still fall for that email.
He fell for the oldest trick in the book.
I have fallen for worse scams.

senses.head: Fall back on — resort to
body: Of the reserve you turn to when the first choice fails: savings, an old job, a familiar excuse. (прибегать к, опираться на (запасной вариант))
examples: It helps to have savings to fall back on.
She fell back on her old job.
They have fallen back on the same excuse all year.

entries.register: everyday — one of the verbs an American uses without thinking
entries.contrast: Fall takes no object: not he fell the glass but he dropped the glass. The separate verb fell meaning to cut down a tree is regular (felled, felled), which is why the past fell and that verb look alike. And not I have fell — the participle is fallen.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; also linking (copular) in the fixed fall asleep, fall ill, fall silent, fall in love, where an adjective or phrase follows instead of an object.
entries.transitivity: intransitive in every sense, and this is the trap: ✗ he fell the glass — you drop a glass, or fell a tree with the separate regular verb fell, felled.
entries.passive: no — nothing can be promoted: ✗ the capital was fallen in three days. The fallen is a noun from the participle, not a passive.
entries.phrasal verbs: fall apart · fall back · fall back on · fall behind · fall down · fall for · fall in · fall in with · fall off · fall on · fall out · fall through · fall under

entries.meaning: To move through the air; to travel in or pilot an aircraft; and, of time and people, to move very fast.
examples: Geese fly south along the river every October.
A hawk flew low over the field.
Sparks have flown into the dry grass.
I fly out Sunday night.
We flew to Denver on Tuesday morning.
She has flown this route a hundred times.
She flies cargo runs to Alaska.
The copilot flew the last leg.
He has flown small planes since he was nineteen.
Time flies when the work is interesting.
The morning flew by.
The whole week has flown past.
Ships fly the flag of the country they are registered in.
Kids flew kites all afternoon out on the point.
The embassy has flown the flag at half staff all week.
Families fly the city at the first sign of trouble.
He flew the country before the indictment.
Many have flown to the hills for safety.
He flies off the handle over nothing.
She flew off the handle at the dispatcher.
He has flown off the handle twice this week.
He tends to fly out to left.
She flied out to end the inning.
The cleanup hitter has flied out three times tonight.

senses.head: Move through the air
body: The core sense, of birds, insects, and anything airborne. (летать, лететь)
examples: Geese fly south along the river every October.
A hawk flew low over the field.
Sparks have flown into the dry grass.

senses.head: Travel by plane
body: Of the passenger rather than the pilot. Not I have flew — the participle is flown. (летать самолётом, лететь)
examples: I fly out Sunday night.
We flew to Denver on Tuesday morning.
She has flown this route a hundred times.

senses.head: Pilot an aircraft
body: Transitive, with the aircraft as the object: fly a plane, fly cargo. (пилотировать, управлять самолётом)
examples: She flies cargo runs to Alaska.
The copilot flew the last leg.
He has flown small planes since he was nineteen.

senses.head: Move fast, rush by
body: Very common with time as the subject: time flies, the week flew by. (мчаться, лететь (о времени))
examples: Time flies when the work is interesting.
The morning flew by.
The whole week has flown past.

senses.head: Fly a flag, fly a kite
body: Transitive, of something held up in the wind — a flag, a kite, a banner. (поднимать флаг; запускать змея)
examples: Ships fly the flag of the country they are registered in.
Kids flew kites all afternoon out on the point.
The embassy has flown the flag at half staff all week.

senses.head: Flee, get away
body: Literary and legal, and old-fashioned in speech; ordinary English uses flee, fled. (спасаться бегством, бежать)
examples: Families fly the city at the first sign of trouble.
He flew the country before the indictment.
Many have flown to the hills for safety.

senses.head: Fly off the handle — lose your temper
body: Informal and fixed; the handle never varies. (вспылить, сорваться)
examples: He flies off the handle over nothing.
She flew off the handle at the dispatcher.
He has flown off the handle twice this week.

senses.head: Baseball: hit a fly ball
body: In this sense only, the verb is regular: flied out, never flew out. (выбить мяч свечой (бейсбол))
examples: He tends to fly out to left.
She flied out to end the inning.
The cleanup hitter has flied out three times tonight.

entries.register: everyday — one of the verbs an American uses without thinking
entries.contrast: In baseball the verb is regular: a batter flied out, never flew out. Everywhere else it is flew and flown, so not I have flew. The past flew is a homophone of flu and flue.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, of birds, aircraft, time, and tempers.
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive of motion (geese fly south, we flew to Denver, time flies), transitive when you pilot or hoist something (she flies cargo runs, ships fly the flag) or flee a place (he flew the country).
entries.passive: yes in the transitive senses — the flag has been flown at half staff all week, the last leg was flown by the copilot. No passive of we flew to Denver.
entries.phrasal verbs: fly at · fly by · fly out

entries.meaning: To order that something not be done.
examples: Parents who forbid everything get obeyed least.
The judge forbade any contact with the witness.
Her doctor had forbidden coffee for a month.
Most parks forbid open fires in August.
State law forbade the sale outright.
The lease has forbidden subletting from the start.
God forbid anything happens to that bridge.
Heaven forbid she find out from a stranger.

senses.head: Order someone not to do something
body: With a personal object plus to or from — forbade him to leave, forbade him from leaving — but never a bare infinitive. (запрещать кому-л. делать что-л.)
examples: Parents who forbid everything get obeyed least.
The judge forbade any contact with the witness.
Her doctor had forbidden coffee for a month.

senses.head: Of a rule or law: prohibit
body: With an inanimate subject — a rule, a lease, a statute — and usually no personal object at all. (запрещать (о правиле, законе, договоре))
examples: Most parks forbid open fires in August.
State law forbade the sale outright.
The lease has forbidden subletting from the start.

senses.head: God forbid, heaven forbid
body: A frozen exclamation using the old subjunctive; the verb takes no other form inside it. (не дай бог, упаси боже)
examples: God forbid anything happens to that bridge.
Heaven forbid she find out from a stranger.

entries.register: everyday — forbidden is in constant use, and God forbid is a fixed phrase
entries.contrast: Built on bid, but only on its command sense, so the strong forms are the normal ones here. Americans usually say forbade as /fərˈbæd/, rhyming with had. It takes to or from — forbade him to leave, forbade him from leaving — but never a bare infinitive: not forbade him leave.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, a verb of ordering; the subject can also be an inanimate rule or law.
entries.transitivity: transitive, with a personal object plus to or from (forbade him to leave, forbade him from leaving) or with a bare object (most parks forbid open fires). Never a bare infinitive: ✗ forbade him leave.
entries.passive: yes, and the participle is everywhere as an adjective — subletting is forbidden by the lease, he was forbidden to leave the state.

entries.meaning: To know or expect in advance that something will happen.
examples: Few economists foresee a sharp drop this year.
Nobody foresaw how fast the neighborhood would change.
We have foreseen most of these problems.
She foresees trouble with the schedule.
Good contracts foresee the obvious disputes.
The engineers had foreseen the flaw but were overruled.
No one had foreseen a delay that long.

senses.head: Predict, expect in advance
body: Of trends, outcomes, and events. Often negative: nobody foresaw, no one could have foreseen. (предвидеть, предугадывать)
examples: Few economists foresee a sharp drop this year.
Nobody foresaw how fast the neighborhood would change.
We have foreseen most of these problems.
She foresees trouble with the schedule.

senses.head: Anticipate and plan for
body: Engineering and legal use, where the adjective foreseeable does much of the work: the foreseeable future, foreseeable risk. (предусматривать, учитывать заранее)
examples: Good contracts foresee the obvious disputes.
The engineers had foreseen the flaw but were overruled.
No one had foreseen a delay that long.

entries.register: neutral to formal — ordinary in writing, less common in speech
entries.contrast: Built on see and inflected exactly like it: foresaw, foreseen. The common adjective is foreseeable, as in the foreseeable future.
entries.verb type: stative — a mental verb of knowing in advance, so it stays out of the progressive: ✗ I am foreseeing trouble; say I foresee trouble.
entries.transitivity: transitive, with a noun or a clause as the object — few economists foresee a sharp drop, nobody foresaw how fast it would change.
entries.passive: yes — unusual for a stative verb, but natural here: the flaw had been foreseen but overruled, a delay that long could not have been foreseen.

entries.meaning: To stop being angry at someone for what they did; in finance, to cancel a debt.
examples: Some people forgive easily; others never do.
She forgave him after a long talk on the porch.
I have forgiven worse than that.
My grandmother forgives everyone but the phone company.
The program forgives the balance after ten years of payments.
He had forgiven the debt years earlier.
The bank has forgiven part of the loan.
Forgive me for asking, but how much did it cost?
You will forgive the mess — we just moved in.

senses.head: Pardon, stop being angry
body: The core sense. You forgive a person, or you forgive the person for the act: forgive him for lying. (прощать)
examples: Some people forgive easily; others never do.
She forgave him after a long talk on the porch.
I have forgiven worse than that.
My grandmother forgives everyone but the phone company.

senses.head: Cancel a debt
body: Financial and quite literal: the money no longer has to be repaid. Loan forgiveness is the standard noun. (списывать долг, прощать задолженность)
examples: The program forgives the balance after ten years of payments.
He had forgiven the debt years earlier.
The bank has forgiven part of the loan.

senses.head: Forgive me — polite formula
body: A set softener before an interruption, a blunt question, or an apology for a mess. (простите, извините)
examples: Forgive me for asking, but how much did it cost?
You will forgive the mess — we just moved in.

entries.register: everyday — one of the verbs an American uses without thinking
entries.contrast: Built on give and inflected exactly like it. Not I have forgave — the participle is forgiven. In finance it keeps its literal force: the bank forgave the debt means it canceled it.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; a change of attitude rather than a state, so the progressive is fine (she is forgiving him slowly).
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive in some people forgive easily, transitive with a person or a debt (she forgave him, the bank forgave the loan), and ditransitive in the older forgive us our debts.
entries.passive: yes — part of the loan has been forgiven, he was never really forgiven for it.
entries.phrasal verbs: forgive for

entries.meaning: To abandon someone or something completely.
examples: Good friends do not forsake you when things go wrong.
The old hymn says he never forsakes his people.
Her sons had forsaken the farm long before she died.
He forsook the city for a cabin in Maine.
She has forsaken sugar entirely.
The settlers had forsaken the valley by 1890.
They have forsaken a plan they spent a year building.

senses.head: Abandon a person
body: Formal and literary, common in hymns and vows. Everyday American speech says abandon or walk out on. (покидать, бросать (кого-л.))
examples: Good friends do not forsake you when things go wrong.
The old hymn says he never forsakes his people.
Her sons had forsaken the farm long before she died.

senses.head: Give up a place, habit, or plan
body: With a thing rather than a person. The participle also works as a plain adjective: a forsaken little town. (отказываться от, оставлять (что-л.))
examples: He forsook the city for a cabin in Maine.
She has forsaken sugar entirely.
The settlers had forsaken the valley by 1890.
They have forsaken a plan they spent a year building.

entries.register: formal — literary; hymns and vows, where speech says abandon
entries.contrast: Follows the take pattern — forsook, forsaken — and never forsaked. It is formal and literary; in everyday American speech you would say abandon or give up on. The participle also stands alone as an adjective: a forsaken little town.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, a verb of abandoning; formal and literary in register.
entries.transitivity: transitive in both senses, and the object is obligatory — he forsook the city, good friends do not forsake you. ✗ her sons had forsaken on its own.
entries.passive: yes — the valley had been forsaken by 1890. The participle also stands alone as an adjective: a forsaken little town.

entries.meaning: To hand something over or provide it — plus a large family of idioms from give up to give birth.
examples: They give every new hire a week of training.
He gave me his number on a napkin.
She has given me the keys already.
Alumni give to the scholarship fund every spring.
They gave ten thousand dollars to the shelter.
We have given away most of the furniture.
Cheap tires give you nothing but trouble.
The noise gave me a headache.
That trip has given her a whole new plan.
She gives the same talk twice a year.
They gave a party for the retiring dean.
He has given four concerts this month.
The old lock gives if you push hard.
The floorboard gave under his weight.
The rope had given before anyone noticed.
Do not give up this early.
He gave up smoking in his forties.
She has given up on the whole project.
Parents give in faster than they admit.
The union gave in on the pension question.
Management has given in twice already.
Volunteers give out water at every mile.
The batteries gave out halfway through.
His knees have given out.
The store gives away samples on Saturdays.
His face gave him away.
Somebody has given away the ending.
Cows on this farm give birth in early spring.
She gave birth on the way to the hospital.
She has given birth to three boys.
Given the weather, the turnout was good.
Given that nobody objected, we moved on.

senses.head: Hand over, pass to someone
body: The core sense, with two objects: give someone something or give something to someone. (давать, вручать, передавать)
examples: They give every new hire a week of training.
He gave me his number on a napkin.
She has given me the keys already.

senses.head: Donate, contribute
body: Of charity and gifts, often intransitive with to: give to the fund. (жертвовать, дарить)
examples: Alumni give to the scholarship fund every spring.
They gave ten thousand dollars to the shelter.
We have given away most of the furniture.

senses.head: Provide, cause someone to have
body: Give someone trouble, a headache, an idea, a hard time — the subject causes the object to have something, good or bad. (предоставлять; вызывать, доставлять)
examples: Cheap tires give you nothing but trouble.
The noise gave me a headache.
That trip has given her a whole new plan.

senses.head: Give a talk, a party, a performance
body: With an event as the object: the subject is the one putting it on. (выступать с (речью, докладом); устраивать (приём))
examples: She gives the same talk twice a year.
They gave a party for the retiring dean.
He has given four concerts this month.

senses.head: Yield, bend under pressure
body: Intransitive: something bends, stretches, or breaks rather than holding firm. (поддаваться, прогибаться)
examples: The old lock gives if you push hard.
The floorboard gave under his weight.
The rope had given before anyone noticed.

senses.head: Give up — stop trying; surrender
body: Two branches: to quit an effort, and to quit a habit. Give oneself up is to surrender to the police. (сдаваться; бросать (дело, привычку))
examples: Do not give up this early.
He gave up smoking in his forties.
She has given up on the whole project.

senses.head: Give in — yield to pressure
body: To stop resisting a demand, usually after holding out for a while. Often with to. (уступать, сдаваться под давлением)
examples: Parents give in faster than they admit.
The union gave in on the pension question.
Management has given in twice already.

senses.head: Give out — run out; distribute; fail
body: Three related uses: supplies run out, people hand things out, and bodies or machines quit working. (кончаться; раздавать; отказать (о силах))
examples: Volunteers give out water at every mile.
The batteries gave out halfway through.
His knees have given out.

senses.head: Give away — donate; reveal
body: To hand over for nothing, or to let a secret slip. Give away the ending is the standard spoiler warning. (отдавать даром; выдать (секрет))
examples: The store gives away samples on Saturdays.
His face gave him away.
Somebody has given away the ending.

senses.head: Give birth
body: A fixed phrase, with to before the child. Also figurative: the era gave birth to a whole style. (рожать, родить)
examples: Cows on this farm give birth in early spring.
She gave birth on the way to the hospital.
She has given birth to three boys.

senses.head: Given — considering, in view of
body: The participle has hardened into a preposition and conjunction: given the weather, given that we are late. (учитывая, принимая во внимание)
examples: Given the weather, the turnout was good.
Given that nobody objected, we moved on.

entries.register: everyday — one of the verbs an American uses without thinking
entries.contrast: Not he has gave it to me — the participle is given. The vowel is short in the base and the participle (giv, GIV-n) and long only in the past (gave), which is the whole shape of this group in miniature.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic throughout, including the intransitive the floorboard gave under his weight. The participle given has hardened into a preposition in given the weather.
entries.transitivity: ditransitive in the core sense, either order — he gave me his number / he gave his number to me. Also plain transitive (they gave a party) and intransitive (alumni give to the fund, the old lock gives).
entries.passive: yes, and either object can be promoted — she was given the keys already or the keys were given to her. No passive of the floorboard gave.
entries.phrasal verbs: give away · give back · give in · give off · give onto · give out · give over · give up · give up on

entries.meaning: To get bigger over time, to cultivate something that does, and to become — gradually — something else.
examples: Cities grow toward the water first.
He grew four inches over the summer.
The town has grown by half since 2010.
Tomatoes grow well on that side of the house.
She grows herbs on the fire escape.
They have grown the same corn for forty years.
He decided to grow a beard in November.
Her hair had grown past her shoulders.
She has grown it out twice and cut it both times.
People grow impatient in that line.
It grew dark before we reached the car.
The crowd has grown quiet.
They want to grow the company without new debt.
She grew the client list from six to sixty.
He has grown revenue every quarter.
Kids grow up fast around here.
I grew up two towns over.
He has grown up a lot since the fall.
The song grows on you.
The apartment grew on her by August.
That painting has grown on me.
Old friends sometimes grow apart.
They grew apart after the move.
He has grown into the job.

senses.head: Get bigger, increase
body: The core intransitive sense, of people, towns, numbers, and anything that gets larger on its own. (расти, увеличиваться)
examples: Cities grow toward the water first.
He grew four inches over the summer.
The town has grown by half since 2010.

senses.head: Cultivate, raise (plants)
body: Transitive, with a crop or a plant as the object. (выращивать)
examples: Tomatoes grow well on that side of the house.
She grows herbs on the fire escape.
They have grown the same corn for forty years.

senses.head: Let hair or a beard get longer
body: Transitive, often with out: grow it out. (отращивать (волосы, бороду))
examples: He decided to grow a beard in November.
Her hair had grown past her shoulders.
She has grown it out twice and cut it both times.

senses.head: Become, turn gradually
body: With an adjective: grow quiet, grow tired, grow dark. Slightly more formal and slower-sounding than get. (становиться (постепенно))
examples: People grow impatient in that line.
It grew dark before we reached the car.
The crowd has grown quiet.

senses.head: Expand a business
body: Transitive and firmly business register: grow the company, grow revenue. Some editors still dislike it. (развивать, наращивать (бизнес, выручку))
examples: They want to grow the company without new debt.
She grew the client list from six to sixty.
He has grown revenue every quarter.

senses.head: Grow up — become an adult
body: Both about maturing and about where your childhood happened: I grew up two towns over. (взрослеть; расти (где-л.))
examples: Kids grow up fast around here.
I grew up two towns over.
He has grown up a lot since the fall.

senses.head: Grow on someone — become likable
body: Of something you disliked at first and came to enjoy. The subject is the thing, not the person. (начать нравиться со временем)
examples: The song grows on you.
The apartment grew on her by August.
That painting has grown on me.

senses.head: Grow apart, grow into
body: Grow apart is of relationships that fade; grow into is of a role or a piece of clothing you become the right size for. (отдаляться друг от друга; дорасти до)
examples: Old friends sometimes grow apart.
They grew apart after the move.
He has grown into the job.

entries.register: everyday — one of the verbs an American uses without thinking
entries.contrast: Not it has grew — use has grown. The past grew rhymes with do, not with grow. With crops the verb takes an object (they grow corn); in the sense of getting bigger it takes none (the town grew).
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; also linking (copular) in sense 4, where an adjective follows: grow tired, grow dark, the crowd has grown quiet.
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive when something gets bigger on its own (the town has grown by half), transitive when you cultivate or expand something (she grows herbs, he has grown revenue every quarter, grow a beard).
entries.passive: yes in the cultivate and expand senses — the same corn has been grown here for forty years. No passive of the intransitive the town grew or of the linking it grew dark.
entries.phrasal verbs: grow apart · grow back · grow into · grow on · grow out of · grow up
entries.see also: outgrow, overgrow, regrow, know, throw, blow

entries.meaning: To have information about something, to be acquainted with someone, and to be able to tell one thing from another.
examples: They know the neighborhood better than anyone.
I knew the answer and then forgot it.
We had known about the layoffs for weeks.
Do you know the family on the corner?
He knew the city well enough to skip the map.
She has known him since grade school.
He knows three languages.
She knew how to fix the pump herself.
Nobody here has known how to run that machine since he left.
You would know her anywhere by that laugh.
I knew him from his voice before he turned around.
He has known good work from bad since he was twenty.
Few of us know what that is like.
He knew real poverty as a child.
That family has never known a quiet year.
I know of her, but we have never met.
Nobody knew about the second offer.
The board has known about the deficit since spring.
The street is known for its bakeries.
He was known around town as Doc.
The place has been known by three names.

senses.head: Have information, be aware
body: The core sense, with a clause or a fact as the object. Not a progressive verb: not I am knowing. (знать (что-л.))
examples: They know the neighborhood better than anyone.
I knew the answer and then forgot it.
We had known about the layoffs for weeks.

senses.head: Be acquainted with a person or place
body: Of people, cities, and streets you have direct experience of, usually with since or for. (быть знакомым с, знать (кого-л.))
examples: Do you know the family on the corner?
He knew the city well enough to skip the map.
She has known him since grade school.

senses.head: Have a skill, know how to
body: Know how to plus a verb, or know a language or a trade. (уметь, владеть (языком, навыком))
examples: He knows three languages.
She knew how to fix the pump herself.
Nobody here has known how to run that machine since he left.

senses.head: Recognize, tell apart
body: Often know someone by a detail, or know A from B. (узнавать, различать)
examples: You would know her anywhere by that laugh.
I knew him from his voice before he turned around.
He has known good work from bad since he was twenty.

senses.head: Experience, live through
body: Usually in the perfect and often negative: she has never known hunger. Formal and a little literary. (испытать, познать, изведать)
examples: Few of us know what that is like.
He knew real poverty as a child.
That family has never known a quiet year.

senses.head: Know of, know about
body: Weaker than plain know: to have heard of something without direct acquaintance. (слышать о, быть в курсе)
examples: I know of her, but we have never met.
Nobody knew about the second offer.
The board has known about the deficit since spring.

senses.head: Be known as, be known for
body: Passive only. Known as gives a name or role; known for gives what something is famous for. (быть известным как; славиться)
examples: The street is known for its bakeries.
He was known around town as Doc.
The place has been known by three names.

entries.register: everyday — one of the verbs an American uses without thinking
entries.contrast: The k is silent in every form. Not I have knew — the participle is known. Knew /nu/ is a homophone of new, and know of no.
entries.verb type: stative — a verb of cognition, and one of the clearest cases of a verb that rejects the progressive: ✗ I am knowing the answer; say I know the answer.
entries.transitivity: transitive, with a noun, a clause, or how to as the object — they know the neighborhood, she knew how to fix the pump. Weakened with a preposition in I know of her.
entries.passive: restricted — stative, so the plain passive is bad: ✗ the answer is known by me. It survives in fixed frames with no by-phrase: the street is known for its bakeries, he was known around town as Doc, the place has been known by three names.
entries.phrasal verbs: know of

entries.meaning: To be, or move into, a flat resting position; also, to be situated, and to consist in something. (The verb meaning to tell an untruth is a separate, regular verb: lied, lied.)
examples: I lie down for twenty minutes after lunch.
She lay on the couch all afternoon.
The keys have lain on the counter since Friday.
He lay awake until three in the morning.
The town lies just east of the river.
The border lay two hours north of the camp.
The ruins have lain under that field for centuries.
Half the lots lie empty.
The mill lay idle for a decade.
Snow had lain on the field for a week.
The trouble lies in the wiring, not the switch.
The final say lay with the trustees.
The answer has lain in the data all along.
A hard winter lies ahead.
Nobody knew what lay behind the decision.
Whatever had lain behind the delay, no one explained it.

senses.head: Recline, lie down
body: Takes no object. The transitive twin lay, laid, laid means to put something down, which is why I laid down for a nap is the most common error in English — the right form is I lay down. (лежать, ложиться)
examples: I lie down for twenty minutes after lunch.
She lay on the couch all afternoon.
The keys have lain on the counter since Friday.
He lay awake until three in the morning.

senses.head: Be situated (of a place)
body: Of towns, borders, and land relative to something else. Slightly formal but standard in description. (находиться, располагаться)
examples: The town lies just east of the river.
The border lay two hours north of the camp.
The ruins have lain under that field for centuries.

senses.head: Remain in a state — lie idle, lie empty
body: With an adjective: something stays untouched or unused for a long stretch. (оставаться (без дела, пустым, нетронутым))
examples: Half the lots lie empty.
The mill lay idle for a decade.
Snow had lain on the field for a week.

senses.head: Lie in, lie with — consist in; rest with
body: Formal: the problem lies in the wiring, the decision lies with the board. (заключаться в; лежать на (об ответственности))
examples: The trouble lies in the wiring, not the switch.
The final say lay with the trustees.
The answer has lain in the data all along.

senses.head: Lie ahead, lie behind
body: Of what is coming and of what caused something, both common in narrative and news writing. (предстоять; стоять за (чем-л.))
examples: A hard winter lies ahead.
Nobody knew what lay behind the decision.
Whatever had lain behind the delay, no one explained it.

entries.register: everyday — one of the verbs an American uses without thinking, though lain is rare in speech
entries.third person: lies · -ing form: lying (the ie becomes y)
entries.contrast: Two traps at once. First, the transitive twin: lay, laid, laid means to put something down (lay the book here), while lie, lay, lain means to recline — and since the past of lie is spelled lay, the wrong I laid down for a nap is everywhere; the right form is I lay down for a nap. Second, lie meaning to tell an untruth is a regular verb: lied, lied.
entries.verb type: stative in the situated and remaining senses (the town lies east of the river, the mill lay idle) — closer to a position than an act; action only in the moment of lying down. The lie idle / lie empty pattern is effectively linking.
entries.transitivity: intransitive in every sense. Its transitive twin is the separate regular lay, laid, laid: you lay a book down, but ✗ I laid down for a nap — the past of lie is lay: I lay down for a nap.
entries.passive: no — no object exists to promote: ✗ the counter was lain on by the keys. Only the active the keys have lain on the counter.
entries.phrasal verbs: lie around · lie behind · lie in · lie low · lie with

entries.meaning: To take one person or thing to be another, and so to be wrong about it.
examples: People often mistake her for her sister.
I mistook the salt for sugar.
He has mistaken my silence for agreement.
Nobody mistakes him for a beginner anymore.
You are mistaken about the deadline.
If I am not mistaken, she left at six.
He admitted he had been mistaken.
There is no mistaking that voice.
There was no mistaking what he meant.
She had mistaken the date and arrived a day early, but there was no mistaking the invitation.

senses.head: Mistake A for B
body: The pattern is mistake A for B, never mistake A with B. (принимать одно за другое, путать)
examples: People often mistake her for her sister.
I mistook the salt for sugar.
He has mistaken my silence for agreement.
Nobody mistakes him for a beginner anymore.

senses.head: Be mistaken — be wrong
body: A passive-shaped fixed use where the participle is really an adjective: you are mistaken, if I am not mistaken. (ошибаться, заблуждаться)
examples: You are mistaken about the deadline.
If I am not mistaken, she left at six.
He admitted he had been mistaken.

senses.head: There is no mistaking
body: A frozen negative construction meaning something is unmistakable. (нельзя не узнать, невозможно спутать)
examples: There is no mistaking that voice.
There was no mistaking what he meant.
She had mistaken the date and arrived a day early, but there was no mistaking the invitation.

entries.register: everyday — you're mistaken and mistake one for the other are ordinary speech
entries.contrast: Built on take and inflected exactly like it. The pattern is mistake A for B, not mistake A with B. The participle is also a plain adjective: you are mistaken means you are wrong.
