entries.verb type: action — dynamic but mental, a verb of misidentifying; the progressive is rare outside there is no mistaking that voice.
entries.transitivity: transitive, in the fixed frame mistake A for B — I mistook the salt for sugar. Never mistake A with B.
entries.passive: yes — she is often mistaken for her sister. The fixed you are mistaken looks passive but the participle there is a plain adjective meaning wrong.

entries.meaning: To do something better than someone else does it.
examples: The brothers try to outdo each other every Thanksgiving.
Nobody outdoes him at trivia night.
The sequel has outdone the original at the box office.
They had outdone every rival by June.
She outdid herself with the cake this year.
You have really outdone yourself.
He outdoes himself every holiday.
Not to be outdone, the other store cut its prices too.
The neighbors, not to be outdone, outdid the whole block with lights.

senses.head: Surpass, do better than
body: With a rival or a previous version as the object. (превосходить, обходить)
examples: The brothers try to outdo each other every Thanksgiving.
Nobody outdoes him at trivia night.
The sequel has outdone the original at the box office.
They had outdone every rival by June.

senses.head: Outdo oneself
body: Reflexive and always a compliment: to do unusually well by your own standard. (превзойти самого себя)
examples: She outdid herself with the cake this year.
You have really outdone yourself.
He outdoes himself every holiday.

senses.head: Not to be outdone
body: A frozen phrase that introduces whoever answers a display in kind. (не желая отставать)
examples: Not to be outdone, the other store cut its prices too.
The neighbors, not to be outdone, outdid the whole block with lights.

entries.register: neutral — the idiom outdo yourself is common; otherwise mostly written
entries.contrast: Built on do and inflected exactly like it. It is often reflexive: she outdid herself means she did unusually well, not that she competed with herself.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, a verb of surpassing.
entries.transitivity: transitive, and the object is obligatory — a rival, a previous version, or a reflexive: nobody outdoes him at trivia, she outdid herself with the cake. ✗ the sequel has outdone alone.
entries.passive: yes, though mostly in the frozen not to be outdone — the original has been outdone at the box office is fine but less common than the active.

entries.meaning: To grow too big or too old for something, or to grow faster than something else.
examples: Kids outgrow shoes faster than they wear them out.
My son outgrows his jeans every spring.
She has outgrown every coat we bought her.
Most children outgrow the allergy.
He outgrew his fear of dogs.
She has outgrown the tantrums.
A school outgrows its building faster than the district plans for.
The company had outgrown its first office within a year.
They have outgrown the old scheduling system.
The suburbs outgrew the city in a decade.
Demand has outgrown supply.
Costs regularly outgrow the budget that set them.

senses.head: Grow too big for (clothes)
body: The everyday sense, about children and clothing. It always takes an object. (вырастать из (одежды, обуви))
examples: Kids outgrow shoes faster than they wear them out.
My son outgrows his jeans every spring.
She has outgrown every coat we bought her.

senses.head: Grow out of a habit or a fear
body: Of a phase, an allergy, or a fear that goes away as a person gets older. (перерасти, избавиться с возрастом)
examples: Most children outgrow the allergy.
He outgrew his fear of dogs.
She has outgrown the tantrums.

senses.head: Become too big for a place or system
body: Of an organization that no longer fits its building, its tools, or its structure. (перерасти (помещение, систему))
examples: A school outgrows its building faster than the district plans for.
The company had outgrown its first office within a year.
They have outgrown the old scheduling system.

senses.head: Grow faster than something else
body: Comparative use with two things growing at once — demand against supply, suburbs against the city. (расти быстрее, чем)
examples: The suburbs outgrew the city in a decade.
Demand has outgrown supply.
Costs regularly outgrow the budget that set them.

entries.register: everyday — children outgrow clothes and phases; heard constantly
entries.contrast: Built on grow and inflected exactly like it. It always takes an object — you outgrow a coat, a habit, or an office — so not he has outgrown from his fear.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; the change is gradual, but it is still something that happens rather than a state.
entries.transitivity: transitive in every sense, and the object is obligatory — kids outgrow shoes, the company had outgrown its first office. ✗ he has outgrown from his fear.
entries.passive: restricted — natural enough with institutions (the building had been outgrown within a year), stiff with clothes and phases: ? every coat we bought her has been outgrown.

entries.meaning: To do something to excess — and, of food, to cook it too long.
examples: Do not overdo it on your first day back at the gym.
He always overdoes the apologies.
She has overdone the decorations this year.
He overdid the garlic again.
They had overdone the salt in the second batch.
Editors overdo the italics in that series.
Do not overdo the roast — pull it at 130.
The cook had overdone the steak.
Every burger on the tray has been overdone.
The actor overdoes every death scene.
The script overdid the sentiment.
Critics said the film had overdone the twist.

senses.head: Do to excess
body: Very often the fixed overdo it, especially about effort and exercise. (перебарщивать, переусердствовать)
examples: Do not overdo it on your first day back at the gym.
He always overdoes the apologies.
She has overdone the decorations this year.

senses.head: Use too much of an ingredient
body: With the ingredient or element as the object: garlic, salt, cologne, exclamation points. (переложить, перестараться (с чем-л.))
examples: He overdid the garlic again.
They had overdone the salt in the second batch.
Editors overdo the italics in that series.

senses.head: Overcook
body: Usually met as the participle used adjectivally: an overdone steak. (пережарить, переварить)
examples: Do not overdo the roast — pull it at 130.
The cook had overdone the steak.
Every burger on the tray has been overdone.

senses.head: Overplay, exaggerate
body: Of a performance, a script, or an effect pushed past what the material can carry. (переигрывать, утрировать)
examples: The actor overdoes every death scene.
The script overdid the sentiment.
Critics said the film had overdone the twist.

entries.register: everyday — don't overdo it is an ordinary spoken phrase
entries.contrast: Built on do and inflected exactly like it. Overdone is also an everyday adjective for food cooked too long, and overdo is not overdue, which is an adjective meaning late.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, a verb of excess.
entries.transitivity: transitive, and the object is obligatory — most often the empty it (don't overdo it), otherwise an ingredient or an effect (he overdid the garlic, the script overdid the sentiment).
entries.passive: yes — every burger on the tray has been overdone. The participle is an ordinary adjective too: an overdone steak.

entries.meaning: To take more money out of an account than it holds; in criticism, to exaggerate a portrayal.
examples: Students often overdraw their checking accounts in the first month.
He overdrew the account by sixty dollars.
She has overdrawn twice this year.
The account was overdrawn when the check cleared.
My balance has been overdrawn since Tuesday.
The app warns you before you overdraw.
They had overdrawn the account before payday.
Beginning novelists overdraw their villains.
The playwright overdrew the father badly.
Every figure in the book has been overdrawn.

senses.head: Take out more than the balance
body: Banking, with the account as the object. The fee for it is an overdraft. (превысить остаток счёта, уйти в минус)
examples: Students often overdraw their checking accounts in the first month.
He overdrew the account by sixty dollars.
She has overdrawn twice this year.

senses.head: Be overdrawn (of an account)
body: The passive and adjectival form, which is how most Americans actually meet the word. (быть в минусе (о счёте))
examples: The account was overdrawn when the check cleared.
My balance has been overdrawn since Tuesday.
The app warns you before you overdraw.
They had overdrawn the account before payday.

senses.head: Exaggerate a portrayal
body: Literary criticism: an overdrawn character is drawn too broadly to be believed. (утрировать, изображать преувеличенно)
examples: Beginning novelists overdraw their villains.
The playwright overdrew the father badly.
Every figure in the book has been overdrawn.

entries.register: neutral — banking language; Americans meet it chiefly as overdrawn
entries.contrast: Built on draw and inflected exactly like it, never overdrawed. The participle is common as an adjective in two senses: an overdrawn account is short of money, and an overdrawn character is exaggerated.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; in banking, an act with a consequence, and in criticism, a way of portraying.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive with the account or the character as the object (he overdrew the account by sixty dollars), intransitive in the app warns you before you overdraw.
entries.passive: yes, and this is how most Americans meet the word — the account was overdrawn when the check cleared, every figure in the book has been overdrawn.

entries.meaning: To eat more than you should.
examples: It is easy to overeat at a buffet.
We all overate at Thanksgiving.
He has overeaten every night this week.
She felt sick because she had overeaten.
My uncle overeats whenever he is bored.

senses.head: Eat too much
body: It takes no object: not I overate the pie but I ate too much pie, or simply I overate. (переедать, объедаться)
examples: It is easy to overeat at a buffet.
We all overate at Thanksgiving.
He has overeaten every night this week.
She felt sick because she had overeaten.
My uncle overeats whenever he is bored.

entries.register: everyday — ordinary talk about holidays and buffets
entries.contrast: Built on eat and inflected exactly like it. It takes no object: not I overate the pie but I ate too much pie or simply I overate.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, a verb of excess built on eat.
entries.transitivity: intransitive only — ✗ I overate the pie; say I ate too much pie or simply I overate.
entries.passive: no — intransitive, so nothing can be promoted: ✗ the pie was overeaten.

entries.meaning: To cover something with growth; in practice, met almost only as the participle overgrown.
examples: Vines overgrow the fence every summer.
Weeds overgrew the whole lot in two months.
Ivy has overgrown the north wall.
Brush had overgrown the trail long before we tried it.
The yard was completely overgrown.
He is an overgrown kid with a mortgage.
The garden has overgrown since she moved out.

senses.head: Cover with growth
body: Of vines, weeds, moss, and brush spreading over a surface. The plant is the subject, the place is the object. (зарастать, покрывать зарослями)
examples: Vines overgrow the fence every summer.
Weeds overgrew the whole lot in two months.
Ivy has overgrown the north wall.
Brush had overgrown the trail long before we tried it.

senses.head: Overgrown as an adjective
body: The living form of this verb: an overgrown lot, and figuratively an overgrown puppy, too big for its age. (заросший; переросший)
examples: The yard was completely overgrown.
He is an overgrown kid with a mortgage.
The garden has overgrown since she moved out.

entries.register: rare — the finite verb is seldom used; only overgrown is current
entries.contrast: Built on grow and inflected exactly like it. In practice Americans meet only the participle, used as an adjective: an overgrown lot, an overgrown puppy.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in the finite forms, though in practice Americans meet only the participle overgrown used as an adjective (an overgrown lot, an overgrown puppy).
entries.transitivity: transitive — the plant is the subject and the surface is the object: ivy has overgrown the north wall.
entries.passive: yes, and it is the usual form — the fence is overgrown with vines, the yard was completely overgrown, where the participle also reads as a plain adjective.

entries.meaning: To lie on top of something else, most often a layer of rock, tissue, or material resting over another.
examples: Layers of sandstone overlie the coal seam throughout the valley.
A thin film of clay overlay the ash from the eruption.
Volcanic rock has overlain these deposits for millions of years.
The surveyors found that gravel had overlain the old roadbed.
Coroners in that era often ruled that a mother had overlain her child in the night.
The sow overlay two of the piglets before dawn.
Farmers still build rails into the pen so that a sow cannot overlie her litter.

senses.head: Lie on top of, cover
body: The everyday use is technical — geology, anatomy, materials — describing one layer sitting above another. It is transitive and almost never used of a person lying on a bed. (залегать поверх, покрывать (о слое))
examples: Layers of sandstone overlie the coal seam throughout the valley.
A thin film of clay overlay the ash from the eruption.
Volcanic rock has overlain these deposits for millions of years.
The surveyors found that gravel had overlain the old roadbed.

senses.head: Smother by lying on
body: A narrow, mostly historical and medical sense used of a parent or animal that suffocates an infant or a young animal by rolling onto it. You will meet it in old court records and veterinary writing, not in conversation. (задавить (навалившись), придавить)
examples: Coroners in that era often ruled that a mother had overlain her child in the night.
The sow overlay two of the piglets before dawn.
Farmers still build rails into the pen so that a sow cannot overlie her litter.

entries.register: rare — geological and anatomical writing; speech says sit on top of
entries.third person: overlies · -ing form: overlying (the ie becomes y)
entries.contrast: Built on lie, and it carries that verb's trap in a worse form: the past overlay is spelled exactly like the separate regular verb overlay, overlaid (to put one layer over another) and like the noun an overlay. Overlie is mostly geological; for everyday layering Americans say cover or sit on top of.
entries.verb type: stative in the geological sense — a description of how layers sit, not an event: sandstone overlies the coal seam. Action only in the narrow smother by lying on sense.
entries.transitivity: transitive in both senses, unlike its base verb lie — volcanic rock has overlain these deposits, the sow overlay two of the piglets.
entries.passive: yes, and standard in geology — the coal seam is overlain by sandstone throughout the valley. Rare and awkward in the smothering sense.

entries.meaning: To set aside or take precedence over a decision, a rule, or an automatic control.
examples: The Senate can override a veto with a two-thirds vote.
The board overrode the committee's recommendation without much discussion.
Management has overridden the store policy twice this month.
By then the governor had overridden the county's own order.
Safety concerns override the schedule every single time.
Her loyalty to the team overrode any interest in a bigger paycheck.
Convenience has overridden privacy in most of these apps.
You can override the thermostat from the panel in the hallway.
The pilot overrode the autopilot and landed the plane by hand.
Someone had overridden the alarm before the fire started.
Subclasses override the default constructor when they need extra fields.
He overrode the equals method but forgot to update the hash.
The child class has overridden three of the parent's methods.

senses.head: Overrule a decision
body: The core sense: a higher authority cancels a lower one. Standard in politics and business — Congress overrides a veto, a manager overrides a refund denial. (отменять, преодолевать (решение, вето))
examples: The Senate can override a veto with a two-thirds vote.
The board overrode the committee's recommendation without much discussion.
Management has overridden the store policy twice this month.
By then the governor had overridden the county's own order.

senses.head: Take precedence over
body: Used of one concern outweighing another. The subject is usually an abstract noun — safety, cost, loyalty. (быть важнее, перевешивать)
examples: Safety concerns override the schedule every single time.
Her loyalty to the team overrode any interest in a bigger paycheck.
Convenience has overridden privacy in most of these apps.

senses.head: Take manual control of a system
body: Technical: a person or a switch cancels what an automatic system was going to do. The noun override (a manual override) comes straight from this. (переводить на ручное управление, отключать автоматику)
examples: You can override the thermostat from the panel in the hallway.
The pilot overrode the autopilot and landed the plane by hand.
Someone had overridden the alarm before the fire started.

senses.head: Override a method
body: In object-oriented programming, to replace an inherited method with a new definition in a subclass. Everyday vocabulary for any programmer. (переопределять (метод, в программировании))
examples: Subclasses override the default constructor when they need extra fields.
He overrode the equals method but forgot to update the hash.
The child class has overridden three of the parent's methods.

entries.register: neutral — common in technical, legal, and political contexts
entries.third person: overrides · -ing form: overriding (drop the e; keep both r's)
entries.contrast: Built on ride and inflected exactly like it, never overrided. Keep both r's in every form. The noun an override is stressed on the first syllable.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; in sense 2 the subject is abstract (safety concerns override the schedule) but the verb still names an event.
entries.transitivity: transitive in every sense, and the object is obligatory — the Senate can override a veto, subclasses override the default constructor.
entries.passive: yes — the store policy has been overridden twice this month, someone had overridden the alarm.

entries.meaning: To be in charge of work being done by other people and make sure it goes right.
examples: Two engineers oversee the whole assembly line.
She oversaw the renovation from the first permit to the last inspection.
The agency has overseen clinical trials like this for decades.
A federal monitor had overseen the department for three years by then.
He oversaw the whole quarrel from the top of the stairs.
What she had overseen through the window she never repeated to anyone.

senses.head: Supervise, be in charge of
body: The only common sense. It implies broad responsibility rather than hands-on work — you oversee a project but your team does it. (руководить, курировать, надзирать)
examples: Two engineers oversee the whole assembly line.
She oversaw the renovation from the first permit to the last inspection.
The agency has overseen clinical trials like this for decades.
A federal monitor had overseen the department for three years by then.

senses.head: See without being noticed
body: Archaic and now literary, meaning to catch sight of something you were not meant to see. Do not confuse it with overlook, which means to miss something. (подсмотреть, увидеть невзначай)
examples: He oversaw the whole quarrel from the top of the stairs.
What she had overseen through the window she never repeated to anyone.

entries.register: neutral — ordinary in workplace and administrative language
entries.contrast: Built on see and inflected exactly like it. Do not confuse it with overlook, which means either to miss something or to look down on it from above — nearly the opposite of supervising it.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, a verb of supervising; unlike its base see it takes the progressive freely (she is overseeing the renovation).
entries.transitivity: transitive, and the object is obligatory — two engineers oversee the assembly line. ✗ a monitor had overseen for three years.
entries.passive: yes — the department had been overseen by a federal monitor for three years, clinical trials like this have been overseen by the agency for decades.

entries.meaning: To catch up with and pass something, or, of an event or feeling, to come upon someone suddenly.
examples: Faster riders overtake the pack on the final climb.
A gray sedan overtook us just before the bridge.
She has overtaken two runners since the last mile marker.
Streaming revenue will overtake ticket sales within a few years.
China overtook Japan as the second-largest economy in 2010.
Online orders have overtaken walk-in business at both locations.
Panic can overtake even an experienced diver.
Exhaustion overtook him halfway up the trail.
The expedition was overtaken by a blizzard on the second day.
Their careful plan had been overtaken by events long before the vote.
British learners are taught never to overtake on a blind bend.
The lorry overtook the coach on a stretch marked with solid white lines.

senses.head: Catch up and pass
body: Used of vehicles, runners, and anything moving. In American English drivers usually say pass; overtake is the normal word in British driving and in race reporting on both sides. (догнать и обогнать, обойти)
examples: Faster riders overtake the pack on the final climb.
A gray sedan overtook us just before the bridge.
She has overtaken two runners since the last mile marker.

senses.head: Surpass in amount or rank
body: Figurative, about numbers, sales, or standing rather than motion. Very common in business and statistics writing. (превзойти, обогнать (по количеству, по уровню))
examples: Streaming revenue will overtake ticket sales within a few years.
China overtook Japan as the second-largest economy in 2010.
Online orders have overtaken walk-in business at both locations.

senses.head: Come upon suddenly (of events, feelings)
body: The subject is a storm, an emotion, exhaustion, or events in general, and it is often passive: overtaken by events. Always something the person did not control. (настигнуть, охватить, обрушиться на)
examples: Panic can overtake even an experienced diver.
Exhaustion overtook him halfway up the trail.
The expedition was overtaken by a blizzard on the second day.
Their careful plan had been overtaken by events long before the vote.

senses.head: Overtake (British driving)
body: In British road signs and driving rules overtake is the fixed term for passing another car — no overtaking. American road signs say do not pass instead, so the word carries a distinctly British flavor in this context. (обгонять (на дороге, брит.))
examples: British learners are taught never to overtake on a blind bend.
The lorry overtook the coach on a stretch marked with solid white lines.

entries.register: neutral — the figurative use is common in news; for cars Americans say pass
entries.contrast: Built on take and inflected exactly like it. For cars, Americans normally say pass; overtake belongs to British traffic talk and to American writing about rankings, sales, and events that catch up with people.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, whether the subject is a car, a sales figure, or a blizzard.
entries.transitivity: transitive, and the object is obligatory — a gray sedan overtook us, online orders have overtaken walk-in business. ✗ the lorry overtook on the bend takes an object in the British driving use too, though no overtaking is a fixed sign.
entries.passive: yes, and sense 3 is usually passive — the expedition was overtaken by a blizzard, their plan had been overtaken by events.

entries.meaning: To remove a government or system from power by force, or to overturn something established.
examples: Rebel officers tried to overthrow the president in 1974.
A general strike overthrew the military junta within weeks.
The monarchy has been overthrown twice in a single century.
By spring the junta had overthrown the elected assembly.
A single clean experiment can overthrow a theory that stood for decades.
Her findings overthrew the accepted timeline of the migration.
Digital tools have overthrown the old hierarchy of the newsroom.
Young pitchers often overthrow the cutoff man when they rush.
The shortstop overthrew first base and let in the tying run.
He had overthrown his receiver on three straight plays.

senses.head: Remove from power by force
body: The central political sense — a coup, a revolution, an uprising. The object is a ruler, a government, or a regime. (свергать (правительство, режим))
examples: Rebel officers tried to overthrow the president in 1974.
A general strike overthrew the military junta within weeks.
The monarchy has been overthrown twice in a single century.
By spring the junta had overthrown the elected assembly.

senses.head: Overturn a system or idea
body: Figurative and formal: a discovery or argument destroys an accepted framework. Common in writing about science and law. (ниспровергать, опрокидывать (теорию, порядок))
examples: A single clean experiment can overthrow a theory that stood for decades.
Her findings overthrew the accepted timeline of the migration.
Digital tools have overthrown the old hierarchy of the newsroom.

senses.head: Throw past the target (sports)
body: In baseball and football, to throw the ball beyond the player who was supposed to catch it. Domain-specific but common in game commentary. (перебросить (мяч мимо цели))
examples: Young pitchers often overthrow the cutoff man when they rush.
The shortstop overthrew first base and let in the tying run.
He had overthrown his receiver on three straight plays.

entries.register: neutral — history and news writing about governments
entries.contrast: Built on throw and inflected exactly like it. The noun shifts its stress to the front — OH-ver-throh, the overthrow of the government — while the verb keeps it on the last syllable.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, a verb of removing by force.
entries.transitivity: transitive, and the object is obligatory — a government, a theory, or, in sports, the target of a throw: the shortstop overthrew first base.
entries.passive: yes, and the political sense is very often passive — the monarchy has been overthrown twice in a single century, his receiver had been overthrown on three straight plays.

entries.meaning: To write over something that was already there, replacing it — most often data in a file.
examples: Do not overwrite the config file until you have a copy.
The installer overwrote my custom settings.
Someone has overwritten last night's export with an empty file.
By the time we noticed, the backup script had overwritten two weeks of logs.
Medieval scribes would overwrite older parchment to save material.
She overwrote the wrong date in heavier pen.
A later hand had overwritten several lines of the original text.
First novels are overwritten more often than they are underwritten.
The critic said the middle chapters were badly overwritten.
Editors warn students not to overwrite a simple scene.
Her workshop leader had overwritten every scene in his own draft.

senses.head: Replace existing data
body: The dominant modern sense, from computing: new content destroys the old content in the same place. What is overwritten is gone unless it was backed up. (перезаписать, затереть (данные))
examples: Do not overwrite the config file until you have a copy.
The installer overwrote my custom settings.
Someone has overwritten last night's export with an empty file.
By the time we noticed, the backup script had overwritten two weeks of logs.

senses.head: Write on top of existing writing
body: The literal, physical sense — ink over ink, chalk over chalk. Used of manuscripts, forms, and whiteboards. (писать поверх написанного)
examples: Medieval scribes would overwrite older parchment to save material.
She overwrote the wrong date in heavier pen.
A later hand had overwritten several lines of the original text.

senses.head: Write in an overblown style
body: Nearly always met as the participle used as an adjective — overwritten prose. It criticizes writing that is too elaborate for its subject. (писать вычурно, перегружать текст)
examples: First novels are overwritten more often than they are underwritten.
The critic said the middle chapters were badly overwritten.
Editors warn students not to overwrite a simple scene.
Her workshop leader had overwritten every scene in his own draft.

entries.register: neutral — computing; the file was overwritten is routine
entries.third person: overwrites · -ing form: overwriting (drop the e; keep both r's)
entries.contrast: Built on write and inflected exactly like it. Besides the computing sense it means to write too elaborately, and there the participle is the usual form: an overwritten paragraph.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, a verb of replacing.
entries.transitivity: transitive in the data and manuscript senses (the installer overwrote my custom settings); in sense 3 it is used both transitively (don't overwrite a simple scene) and absolutely (first novels are overwritten).
entries.passive: yes, and it is routine in computing — last night's export has been overwritten with an empty file, the middle chapters were badly overwritten.

entries.meaning: To take part in something, to eat or drink one's share of it, or, formally, to have some quality of it.
examples: Guests are welcome to partake of the buffet after the ceremony.
He partook of the wine rather more freely than the others.
None of us had partaken of anything since breakfast.
Students may partake in the ceremony without walking across the stage.
Only a handful of villagers partook in the vote.
She has partaken in every fundraiser since the club opened.
His speeches partake of both the sermon and the stump speech.
The old house partook of a grandeur the street had long lost.
Her paintings have partaken of that stillness from the very beginning.

senses.head: Partake of — eat or drink
body: Formal or jokingly formal, always with of. In everyday speech Americans say have or help yourself to; partake survives in toasts, menus, and dry humor. (отведать, вкушать, употреблять)
examples: Guests are welcome to partake of the buffet after the ceremony.
He partook of the wine rather more freely than the others.
None of us had partaken of anything since breakfast.

senses.head: Partake in — take part in
body: A formal alternative to take part in or participate in, used with an activity. Slightly stiff in ordinary conversation. (участвовать, принимать участие)
examples: Students may partake in the ceremony without walking across the stage.
Only a handful of villagers partook in the vote.
She has partaken in every fundraiser since the club opened.

senses.head: Partake of — have a quality
body: Literary and formal: something shares in the nature of something else. The object is an abstract noun, and it is never used of people eating. (иметь оттенок, отдавать чем-л.)
examples: His speeches partake of both the sermon and the stump speech.
The old house partook of a grandeur the street had long lost.
Her paintings have partaken of that stillness from the very beginning.

entries.register: formal — toasts, menus, and dry humor; speech says have some
entries.contrast: Built on take and inflected exactly like it. It is formal and a little old-fashioned, and it needs a preposition: partake of food and drink, partake in an activity — never a plain object, so not partake the meal.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in the eating and taking-part senses; closer to stative in the formal sense 3, where something shares a quality: his speeches partake of the sermon.
entries.transitivity: intransitive — it always needs a preposition, of for food and qualities, in for activities. ✗ partake the meal; say partake of the meal.
entries.passive: no — there is no direct object to promote: ✗ the buffet was partaken of by the guests. Keep the active, or use take part in.

entries.meaning: To draw something again in a changed form, whether a picture, a boundary, or the terms of a deal.
examples: Please redraw the elevation with the new window heights.
He redrew the whole panel after the editor's note.
By Friday the architect had redrawn the second floor twice.
State legislatures redraw congressional districts after every census.
The 1919 treaties redrew the map of central Europe.
Cheap batteries have redrawn the energy landscape.
The exporter may redraw on the buyer for the unpaid balance plus charges.
The bank redrew on its correspondent in London.
They have redrawn nearly all of the extra payments made last year.

senses.head: Draw again, revise a drawing
body: The plain literal sense, used of sketches, plans, and anything on screen that a program repaints. (перерисовать, начертить заново)
examples: Please redraw the elevation with the new window heights.
He redrew the whole panel after the editor's note.
By Friday the architect had redrawn the second floor twice.

senses.head: Redraw boundaries or a map
body: Political and administrative, about district lines, borders, or territory. Frequently figurative: an event redraws the map of an industry. (перекраивать границы, переделывать карту)
examples: State legislatures redraw congressional districts after every census.
The 1919 treaties redrew the map of central Europe.
Cheap batteries have redrawn the energy landscape.

senses.head: Redraw a bill or funds (finance)
body: A banking term: to draw a fresh bill of exchange back on a drawer whose bill was dishonored, and, in some mortgage products, to take back extra payments you had already made. Technical and rare outside finance. (выставить обратный вексель; повторно снять средства)
examples: The exporter may redraw on the buyer for the unpaid balance plus charges.
The bank redrew on its correspondent in London.
They have redrawn nearly all of the extra payments made last year.

entries.register: neutral — maps, districts, and boundaries; mostly written
entries.contrast: Built on draw and inflected exactly like it. The Russian gloss here points to an old banking sense (drawing a new bill of exchange); in ordinary American English redraw simply means to draw again, and its commonest use is political: redraw district lines.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, a verb of doing again.
entries.transitivity: transitive in the drawing and boundary senses (legislatures redraw congressional districts); intransitive with on in the banking sense: the bank redrew on its correspondent in London.
entries.passive: yes — congressional districts are redrawn after every census, the second floor had been redrawn twice by Friday.

entries.meaning: To grow again after being cut, lost, or destroyed, or to make something grow again.
examples: Lizard tails regrow, but never quite the way they were.
Her hair regrew within a year of the treatment.
The prairie grass has regrown over the burn scar.
By the second spring the hedge had regrown above the fence line.
You can regrow scallions from the roots in a glass of water.
Researchers regrew the cartilage on a printed scaffold.
The town has regrown its tree canopy since the storm.

senses.head: Grow back (intransitive)
body: The usual sense: hair, leaves, nerves, or forest returning on its own after loss. (отрастать, вырастать заново)
examples: Lizard tails regrow, but never quite the way they were.
Her hair regrew within a year of the treatment.
The prairie grass has regrown over the burn scar.
By the second spring the hedge had regrown above the fence line.

senses.head: Grow again (transitive)
body: With an object — a person or a lab makes something grow back. Common in horticulture and in tissue-engineering writing. (выращивать заново, восстанавливать)
examples: You can regrow scallions from the roots in a glass of water.
Researchers regrew the cartilage on a printed scaffold.
The town has regrown its tree canopy since the storm.

entries.register: neutral — gardening and medicine; ordinary in writing
entries.contrast: Built on grow and inflected exactly like it. It works with an object in gardening and medicine (regrow cartilage) and without one for the thing coming back (the lawn regrew). Written solid, with no hyphen, in American usage.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, of growth returning after loss.
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive when the thing comes back on its own (her hair regrew within a year), transitive when someone makes it come back (you can regrow scallions from the roots).
entries.passive: yes in the transitive sense — the cartilage was regrown on a printed scaffold. No passive of the intransitive the prairie grass has regrown.

entries.meaning: To take something again — a place captured back, an exam sat a second time, a shot filmed over.
examples: Their plan was to retake the ridge before dawn.
Allied forces retook the port in a single night.
The team has retaken first place in the division.
By August the army had retaken most of the province.
Most students retake the exam at least once.
He retook chemistry over the summer.
She has retaken the driving test three times.
The director wanted to retake the whole dinner scene.
They retook the final shot after the light changed.
The crew had retaken that entrance eleven times.
Shareholders moved to retake control of the board.
The lender retook possession of the building.
She has retaken the initiative in every negotiation since.

senses.head: Recapture, take back
body: Military and competitive: to win back a position, city, or lead that had been lost. (снова захватить, отбить обратно)
examples: Their plan was to retake the ridge before dawn.
Allied forces retook the port in a single night.
The team has retaken first place in the division.
By August the army had retaken most of the province.

senses.head: Take a test or course again
body: Everyday academic use. American students retake the SAT; the noun is a retake. (пересдавать (экзамен), проходить курс заново)
examples: Most students retake the exam at least once.
He retook chemistry over the summer.
She has retaken the driving test three times.

senses.head: Film a scene again
body: From film and photography: to shoot the same material over because the first attempt failed. (переснять (дубль, сцену))
examples: The director wanted to retake the whole dinner scene.
They retook the final shot after the light changed.
The crew had retaken that entrance eleven times.

senses.head: Regain control or possession
body: Figurative, about control, initiative, or property returning to its earlier holder. (вернуть себе, снова взять под контроль)
examples: Shareholders moved to retake control of the board.
The lender retook possession of the building.
She has retaken the initiative in every negotiation since.

entries.русский: забирать; снова взять, занять или захватить
entries.register: everyday — students retake a test or a class
entries.contrast: Built on take and inflected exactly like it. The noun a retake — a second filming or a second try at a test — puts the stress on the first syllable: REE-tayk.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, a verb of taking again.
entries.transitivity: transitive, and the object is obligatory — allied forces retook the port, he retook chemistry over the summer, they retook the final shot.
entries.passive: yes — the port was retaken in a single night, the exam can be retaken once.

entries.meaning: To write something again in a different form, or to change what was previously established.
examples: I rewrite the opening paragraph more times than the rest of the piece.
She rewrote the ending after the first table read.
By the deadline he had rewritten every chapter but the last.
A single find can rewrite the history of the region.
That season rewrote the record books for the franchise.
Officials have rewritten the rules three times this year.
We should rewrite the parser instead of patching it again.
They rewrote the backend in Go over one quarter.
The team has rewritten that module from scratch twice.

senses.head: Write again, revise
body: The core sense: producing a new version of a text. Stronger than edit — a rewrite starts over rather than patching. (переписать, переработать (текст))
examples: I rewrite the opening paragraph more times than the rest of the piece.
She rewrote the ending after the first table read.
By the deadline he had rewritten every chapter but the last.

senses.head: Rewrite the rules, history, record books
body: A set of fixed figurative phrases. Rewrite history can be neutral (new evidence) or accusatory (distorting the past); context decides. (переписать (правила, историю, рекорды))
examples: A single find can rewrite the history of the region.
That season rewrote the record books for the franchise.
Officials have rewritten the rules three times this year.

senses.head: Rewrite code
body: Standard in software: replacing an implementation rather than fixing it. Often contrasted with refactor, which preserves the existing structure. (переписать (код, программу))
examples: We should rewrite the parser instead of patching it again.
They rewrote the backend in Go over one quarter.
The team has rewritten that module from scratch twice.

entries.register: everyday — school, work, and any kind of writing
entries.third person: rewrites · -ing form: rewriting (drop the e; keep both r's)
entries.contrast: Built on write and inflected exactly like it. The verb stresses the second syllable, ree-RYTE, while the noun a rewrite stresses the first: REE-ryte.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, a verb of producing a new version.
entries.transitivity: transitive, with a text, a rule, or a body of code as the object — she rewrote the ending, they rewrote the backend in Go.
entries.passive: yes — the rules have been rewritten three times this year, that module has been rewritten from scratch twice.

entries.meaning: To sit on and control a horse, bike, or motorcycle, to travel in a vehicle, or, figuratively, to depend on or endure something.
examples: She rides every Saturday at a stable outside town.
He rode bareback across the pasture.
I have ridden that gray mare since she was three.
None of the kids had ridden a horse before that summer.
Most of the staff ride bikes to work.
He rode his motorcycle from Denver to the coast.
She has ridden the same road bike for a decade.
I ride the train into the city three days a week.
We rode the elevator to the top floor in silence.
He has ridden that same commuter line for twenty years.
Gulls ride the updrafts along the cliff without a wingbeat.
The little boat rode the swell better than we expected.
Surfers have ridden this break since the fifties.
A lot of money is riding on the outcome of this hearing.
His whole reputation rode on one paragraph in that report.
Too much has ridden on this single account for too long.
Small firms rarely ride out a downturn this long.
They rode out the hurricane in the basement.
The company has ridden out worse quarters than this one.
Don't ride him about the mistake — he already knows.
The coach rode the rookies all through camp.
Her supervisor has ridden her about the same report for weeks.

senses.head: Ride a horse
body: The oldest sense and still the default when no vehicle is named. Ride here can be transitive (ride a mare) or intransitive (she rides every weekend). (ездить верхом, скакать)
examples: She rides every Saturday at a stable outside town.
He rode bareback across the pasture.
I have ridden that gray mare since she was three.
None of the kids had ridden a horse before that summer.

senses.head: Ride a bike or motorcycle
body: Anything you sit astride takes ride, not drive — a motorcycle is ridden even though it has an engine. (ездить на велосипеде, мотоцикле)
examples: Most of the staff ride bikes to work.
He rode his motorcycle from Denver to the coast.
She has ridden the same road bike for a decade.

senses.head: Travel as a passenger
body: Americans ride the bus, the subway, an elevator, or in the back seat. British English prefers take the bus, and ride in a car means being a passenger, never driving. (ехать (в транспорте, пассажиром))
examples: I ride the train into the city three days a week.
We rode the elevator to the top floor in silence.
He has ridden that same commuter line for twenty years.

senses.head: Ride waves, wind, current
body: Used of surfers, birds, and boats moving on water or air, and of anything carried along by a current. Also of a ship riding at anchor. (скользить, нестись (на волне, на ветру))
examples: Gulls ride the updrafts along the cliff without a wingbeat.
The little boat rode the swell better than we expected.
Surfers have ridden this break since the fifties.

senses.head: Be riding on — depend on
body: Almost always in the continuous with an abstract subject: money, jobs, or a reputation is riding on an outcome. A fixed pattern rather than a free use. (зависеть от, быть поставленным на карту)
examples: A lot of money is riding on the outcome of this hearing.
His whole reputation rode on one paragraph in that report.
Too much has ridden on this single account for too long.

senses.head: Ride out — get through safely
body: To survive a storm, a downturn, or a scandal by holding on until it passes. The object is a period of trouble. (переждать, пережить (бурю, кризис))
examples: Small firms rarely ride out a downturn this long.
They rode out the hurricane in the basement.
The company has ridden out worse quarters than this one.

senses.head: Ride someone — nag, pressure
body: Informal American English: to criticize or push a person relentlessly. Always with a person as the object. (придираться, наседать (разг.))
examples: Don't ride him about the mistake — he already knows.
The coach rode the rookies all through camp.
Her supervisor has ridden her about the same report for weeks.

entries.register: everyday — one of the verbs an American uses without thinking
entries.contrast: Not I have rode — the participle is ridden. The past rode is a homophone of road and rowed, and the whole family behaves the same way: compare stride and override.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in every sense, including the fixed a lot of money is riding on the outcome, which lives almost entirely in the progressive.
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive in she rides every Saturday, transitive with an animal, a vehicle, a wave, or a person (he rode his motorcycle, I ride the train, the coach rode the rookies). Prepositional in riding on and ride out.
entries.passive: yes in the transitive senses — that gray mare has been ridden since she was three, this break has been ridden since the fifties. No passive of she rides every Saturday.
entries.phrasal verbs: ride on · ride out · ride up

entries.meaning: To move upward, to increase, to get up, or to advance in position — always without an object.
examples: Steam rises off the pavement after a summer storm.
The moon rose behind the ridge just after nine.
The river has risen two feet since midnight.
By morning the water had risen over the doorsill.
Rents rise faster here than wages do.
Unemployment rose sharply in the fall.
Costs have risen every year since the merger.
Farmers here rise before five most of the year.
The whole room rose when the judge came in.
He had risen and dressed before anyone else was awake.
Few analysts rise to partner in under a decade.
She rose through the ranks from dispatcher to chief.
He has risen from stock clerk to regional manager.
When the tax was announced, whole provinces rose against the crown.
The peasants rose up in the spring of that year.
The city has risen against its own council twice in living memory.
Nobody knows who will rise to the occasion until the day comes.
She rose to the challenge and finished the season as captain.
He has risen above worse insults than that one.
Let the dough rise for an hour in a warm kitchen.
The land rose steeply behind the barn.
The Rhine rises in the Swiss Alps.
The loaves had risen well past the rim of the pans.

senses.head: Move upward
body: The literal sense, used of smoke, the sun, water, or land. It never takes an object — you raise a thing, but a thing rises by itself. (подниматься, всходить)
examples: Steam rises off the pavement after a summer storm.
The moon rose behind the ridge just after nine.
The river has risen two feet since midnight.
By morning the water had risen over the doorsill.

senses.head: Increase in amount
body: Used of prices, temperatures, numbers, and levels. Neutral and extremely common in news and business writing. (расти, повышаться (о ценах, числах))
examples: Rents rise faster here than wages do.
Unemployment rose sharply in the fall.
Costs have risen every year since the merger.

senses.head: Get up from bed
body: Formal or literary for people; get up is the everyday choice. It survives in fixed contexts: all rise in a courtroom, rise and shine, rise early. (вставать (с постели, со стула))
examples: Farmers here rise before five most of the year.
The whole room rose when the judge came in.
He had risen and dressed before anyone else was awake.

senses.head: Advance in rank or standing
body: About careers and reputations, often with to or through: rise to the top, rise through the ranks. (продвигаться, достигать высот)
examples: Few analysts rise to partner in under a decade.
She rose through the ranks from dispatcher to chief.
He has risen from stock clerk to regional manager.

senses.head: Rise up — rebel
body: Political, usually rise up against a ruler or a system. Formal and a little dramatic in tone. (восставать, подниматься на борьбу)
examples: When the tax was announced, whole provinces rose against the crown.
The peasants rose up in the spring of that year.
The city has risen against its own council twice in living memory.

senses.head: Rise to the occasion
body: A fixed idiom: to meet a difficult moment with unexpected strength. Also rise to the challenge and rise above (refuse to be dragged down by pettiness). (оказаться на высоте, справиться)
examples: Nobody knows who will rise to the occasion until the day comes.
She rose to the challenge and finished the season as captain.
He has risen above worse insults than that one.

senses.head: Dough, land, a river's source
body: Three related specialized uses: bread dough swells, land slopes upward, and a river rises in the place where it begins. (подниматься (о тесте); брать начало (о реке))
examples: Let the dough rise for an hour in a warm kitchen.
The land rose steeply behind the barn.
The Rhine rises in the Swiss Alps.
The loaves had risen well past the rim of the pans.

entries.register: everyday — one of the verbs an American uses without thinking
entries.contrast: Rise never takes an object; raise (regular: raised, raised) always does. Not he rose the flag but he raised the flag or the flag rose. And not prices have rose — the participle is risen. The past rose is spelled like the flower.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, of upward movement, increase, and advancement.
entries.transitivity: intransitive only, in every sense — the counterpart raise (regular: raised, raised) is the transitive one. ✗ he rose the flag; say he raised the flag or the flag rose.
entries.passive: no — nothing to promote: ✗ the water was risen over the doorsill. Only the active the water had risen over the doorsill.
entries.phrasal verbs: rise above · rise to · rise up

entries.meaning: To perceive with the eyes, and, by extension, to understand, to meet, to experience, or to make sure of something.
examples: I see three deer at the edge of the field.
She saw the taillights turn onto the gravel road.
Nobody has seen that comet since 1997.
He had seen the letter long before he admitted it.
I see what you mean about the second paragraph.
It took a week before anyone saw the flaw in the argument.
Now that you explain it, I have finally seen the logic of it.
You should see a doctor about that cough.
I saw my lawyer on Tuesday about the lease.
She has seen three specialists and gotten three answers.
They have been seeing each other since March.
She was seeing somebody from the office at the time.
He does not see anyone seriously these days.
Let's see the late show instead.
We saw the Cubs play in the rain.
I have seen that movie four times.
Please see that the doors are locked at closing.
The super saw to the leak the same afternoon.
Someone has seen to the paperwork already.
The next ten years will see the whole industry reorganized.
The 1990s saw a wave of small presses open and close.
This town has seen three floods since I moved here.
We always see the grandparents off at the gate.
He saw her home through the rain.
The whole family had seen him off at the pier.
Voters see through that kind of promise immediately.
She saw the project through despite losing half her staff.
He has seen through every excuse I have ever offered.
I see the delay as a chance to test it properly.
Critics saw the film as an apology for the war.
I never saw what she saw in him.
Investors have seen real potential in the smaller markets.

senses.head: Perceive with the eyes
body: The base sense. It describes perception, not deliberate attention, so it is normally not used in the continuous: I see it, not I am seeing it. (видеть, замечать)
examples: I see three deer at the edge of the field.
She saw the taillights turn onto the gravel road.
Nobody has seen that comet since 1997.
He had seen the letter long before he admitted it.

senses.head: Understand, grasp
body: Very common, from I see as an acknowledgment to see the point. The object is an idea rather than a thing. (понимать, видеть (смысл))
examples: I see what you mean about the second paragraph.
It took a week before anyone saw the flaw in the argument.
Now that you explain it, I have finally seen the logic of it.

senses.head: Meet with, consult
body: Used of appointments and visits — see a doctor, see a client. The professional you consult is the object. (встречаться с, обращаться к (врачу, юристу))
examples: You should see a doctor about that cough.
I saw my lawyer on Tuesday about the lease.
She has seen three specialists and gotten three answers.

senses.head: Be seeing someone — date
body: Romantic, and one of the few uses of see that does take the continuous. Are you seeing anyone? is the standard way to ask about someone's relationship status. (встречаться (с кем-л., о романтических отношениях))
examples: They have been seeing each other since March.
She was seeing somebody from the office at the time.
He does not see anyone seriously these days.

senses.head: Watch a movie, game, or show
body: For a one-time event you see a film or a game; for regular viewing of television you watch. Have you seen it? is the standard question about a movie. (смотреть, посмотреть (фильм, спектакль))
examples: Let's see the late show instead.
We saw the Cubs play in the rain.
I have seen that movie four times.

senses.head: See to it — make sure
body: A fixed pattern for taking responsibility that something happens: see to it that, see that, or see to a task. (позаботиться, проследить, чтобы)
examples: Please see that the doors are locked at closing.
The super saw to the leak the same afternoon.
Someone has seen to the paperwork already.

senses.head: Witness, experience (of a period)
body: The subject is a period, a place, or a thing rather than a person: the decade saw enormous change. Standard in journalism and history writing. (видеть, знавать, быть свидетелем (об эпохе, месте))
examples: The next ten years will see the whole industry reorganized.
The 1990s saw a wave of small presses open and close.
This town has seen three floods since I moved here.

senses.head: See someone off, see someone home
body: To go with a person to their point of departure or destination. See off is at a station or airport; see home is walking someone back. (проводить (кого-л.))
examples: We always see the grandparents off at the gate.
He saw her home through the rain.
The whole family had seen him off at the pier.

senses.head: See through — not be fooled
body: Two related fixed uses: see through a person or a lie means you are not deceived; see something through means you stay with a task to the end. (видеть насквозь; довести до конца)
examples: Voters see through that kind of promise immediately.
She saw the project through despite losing half her staff.
He has seen through every excuse I have ever offered.

senses.head: See as, see in — regard
body: With as it means consider or interpret; with in it asks what quality someone finds attractive or promising in another. (считать, воспринимать как; находить (в ком-л.))
examples: I see the delay as a chance to test it properly.
Critics saw the film as an apology for the war.
I never saw what she saw in him.
Investors have seen real potential in the smaller markets.

entries.register: everyday — one of the verbs an American uses without thinking
entries.contrast: I seen it is the classic nonstandard slip: say I saw it or I have seen it. After see, a second verb takes the bare infinitive or -ing form — I saw him leave, I saw him leaving — never I saw him to leave.
entries.verb type: stative in the core perception and understanding senses, so it normally avoids the progressive: ✗ I am seeing three deer. The dating sense is the exception and is dynamic: they have been seeing each other since March.
entries.transitivity: transitive with a noun, a clause, or a bare infinitive or -ing complement — I saw him leave, I saw him leaving, never ✗ I saw him to leave. Prepositional in see to it that.
entries.passive: yes — unusually for a stative verb, it passivizes freely: that comet has not been seen since 1997, the film was seen as an apology for the war.
entries.phrasal verbs: see about · see off · see out · see through · see to

entries.meaning: To move quickly back and forth, to tremble, or to unsettle someone badly.
examples: Shake the bottle well before pouring.
He shook the sand out of his shoes.
The wind has shaken the last apples loose.
Someone had shaken the vending machine hard enough to dent it.
My hands shake whenever I have to speak in public.
The whole house shook when the truck went by.
The windows have shaken like that since the mine reopened.
In this business you shake hands and the deal is done.
They shook hands and never spoke again.
We had shaken on the price before the paperwork arrived.
He just shakes his head whenever the topic comes up.
She shook her head and went back to her book.
The doctor had shaken his head before saying a word.
Bad reviews do not shake him at all.
The accident shook everyone on the crew.
Her confidence has been shaken by two rejections in a row.
I cannot shake off this cold.
He shook off the tackler and went in for the score.
She has never quite shaken off the reputation she got that year.
New owners always shake up the front office.
The near miss shook him up more than he let on.
Management has shaken up the department twice this year.

senses.head: Move something back and forth
body: Transitive and literal — bottles, blankets, trees, a fist. This is the sense behind the label on medicine bottles. (трясти, встряхивать, взбалтывать)
examples: Shake the bottle well before pouring.
He shook the sand out of his shoes.
The wind has shaken the last apples loose.
Someone had shaken the vending machine hard enough to dent it.

senses.head: Tremble, vibrate
body: Intransitive: the subject moves on its own, from cold, fear, laughter, or a passing train. (дрожать, трястись)
examples: My hands shake whenever I have to speak in public.
The whole house shook when the truck went by.
The windows have shaken like that since the mine reopened.

senses.head: Shake hands
body: A fixed social use, alone or with on it to mark an agreement: let's shake on it. (пожать руку)
examples: In this business you shake hands and the deal is done.
They shook hands and never spoke again.
We had shaken on the price before the paperwork arrived.

senses.head: Shake one's head
body: Another fixed collocation. In American culture shaking the head means no or disbelief, and nodding means yes. (качать головой (в знак несогласия))
examples: He just shakes his head whenever the topic comes up.
She shook her head and went back to her book.
The doctor had shaken his head before saying a word.

senses.head: Upset, unsettle
body: Figurative, about emotions and confidence. Very often passive — she was badly shaken — and also used of shaking someone's faith or belief. (потрясти, выбить из колеи)
examples: Bad reviews do not shake him at all.
The accident shook everyone on the crew.
Her confidence has been shaken by two rejections in a row.

senses.head: Shake off — get rid of
body: To free yourself from an illness, a mood, a follower, or a defender. Common in both everyday speech and sports commentary. (избавиться от, стряхнуть)
examples: I cannot shake off this cold.
He shook off the tackler and went in for the score.
She has never quite shaken off the reputation she got that year.

senses.head: Shake up — reorganize; jolt
body: Two senses of the same phrasal verb: to reorganize an institution drastically, or to shock a person. The noun a shake-up comes from the first. (перетряхнуть, реорганизовать; встряхнуть)
examples: New owners always shake up the front office.
The near miss shook him up more than he let on.
Management has shaken up the department twice this year.

entries.register: everyday — one of the verbs an American uses without thinking
entries.contrast: Not I have shook — the participle is shaken. Shaken also serves as an adjective for someone badly upset: she looked shaken.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, of literal motion and of emotional jolts alike.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive when you move something (shake the bottle well, he shook the sand out) or unsettle someone (the accident shook the crew), intransitive when the subject trembles on its own (my hands shake, the whole house shook).
entries.passive: yes, and the emotional sense is very often passive — her confidence has been shaken by two rejections, the last apples have been shaken loose. No passive of the house shook.
entries.phrasal verbs: shake down · shake off · shake on · shake out · shake up

entries.meaning: To kill violently, in older and literary language; in modern slang, to impress or amuse enormously.
examples: In the old stories a single knight can slay a dragon.
He slew the giant with a stone from the brook.
Thousands had been slain before the treaty was signed.
Two brothers have been slain on the same block this year.
That story slays me every time you tell it.
Her opening set slew the crowd at the small club.
The comic has slain tougher rooms than this one.
She slays every time she walks a runway.
They absolutely slayed that dance number.
He has slayed on that stage before.

senses.head: Kill violently
body: Literary, biblical, or heroic in tone — dragons, giants, and enemies are slain. Modern news writing keeps it mainly in headlines, where it is short for murdered. (убивать, сражать, умерщвлять)
examples: In the old stories a single knight can slay a dragon.
He slew the giant with a stone from the brook.
Thousands had been slain before the treaty was signed.
Two brothers have been slain on the same block this year.

senses.head: Amuse or impress hugely
body: Informal: you slay me means you are hilarious, and a performer who slays an audience wins it completely. Older slang, but still widely understood. (сражать наповал, покорять)
examples: That story slays me every time you tell it.
Her opening set slew the crowd at the small club.
The comic has slain tougher rooms than this one.

senses.head: Slay — excel (modern slang)
body: Recent slang, especially about fashion and performance: to look or perform outstandingly. In this sense the past is normally the regular slayed, not slew — the strong forms belong to the older senses. (быть на высоте, отжигать (сленг))
examples: She slays every time she walks a runway.
They absolutely slayed that dance number.
He has slayed on that stage before.

entries.register: rare — the strong slew/slain is literary and headline usage; the modern slang sense is regular (slayed)
entries.contrast: The strong forms slew and slain belong to the killing sense, which survives in literature and in headlines (four slain in crash). The slang sense of impressing an audience is regular: she slayed at the audition. Do not confuse the past slew with the noun a slew of, meaning a large number.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in all three senses.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive in the killing and the you slay me senses (he slew the giant, her set slew the crowd), intransitive in the modern slang: they absolutely slayed.
entries.passive: yes for the killing sense, where the passive is the commonest form — thousands had been slain before the treaty, four slain in crash. No passive of the intransitive slang she slays every time.

entries.meaning: To strike a heavy blow, in archaic and biblical language; in living use, mostly as smitten — struck by love or by affliction.
examples: He was smitten with her from the first rehearsal.
Anyone who meets that puppy is smitten immediately.
She had been smitten long before she admitted it to anyone.
The old text warns that the wicked will smite one another.
He smote the table with his fist and walked out.
The angel had smitten the camp before morning.
Plague can smite a whole village in a season.
Conscience smote him halfway home.
The region has been smitten by drought three years running.

senses.head: Be smitten with — infatuated
body: By far the most common modern use, and only in the passive participle: smitten with or smitten by someone. Light and slightly playful in tone. (быть влюблённым, сражённым (кем-л.))
examples: He was smitten with her from the first rehearsal.
Anyone who meets that puppy is smitten immediately.
She had been smitten long before she admitted it to anyone.

senses.head: Strike hard
body: Archaic and biblical, or used for humorous effect. The object is a person or an enemy, and the striker is often God or fate. (поражать, разить, ударять)
examples: The old text warns that the wicked will smite one another.
He smote the table with his fist and walked out.
The angel had smitten the camp before morning.

senses.head: Afflict, strike down
body: Formal or literary, of disease, guilt, or disaster falling on someone. Nearly always passive: smitten by plague, smitten with remorse. (поражать (о болезни, о совести))
examples: Plague can smite a whole village in a season.
Conscience smote him halfway home.
The region has been smitten by drought three years running.

entries.register: archaic — biblical; the only living form is the adjective smitten
entries.contrast: Almost all living American use is the participle smitten as an adjective meaning infatuated: he is smitten with her. The finite forms smite and smote are biblical or deliberately jokey. The variant participle smit exists but is rare.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; archaic in the finite forms, and today alive mainly as the participle smitten used as an adjective meaning infatuated.
entries.transitivity: transitive — the object is a person, an enemy, or a place: he smote the table with his fist, plague can smite a whole village.
entries.passive: yes, and modern use is almost entirely passive — he was smitten with her from the first rehearsal, the region has been smitten by drought three years running.

entries.meaning: To walk with long, decisive steps.
examples: He tends to stride rather than walk when he is angry.
She strode to the front of the room without a note in her hand.
The coach has stridden up and down that sideline for thirty seasons.
By then he had stridden halfway across the lobby.
Long-legged birds stride across the mudflats at low tide.
He strode over the fallen branch without breaking pace.
The hikers had stridden across three fields before noon.
In the old cartoons the magnate seems to stride the whole continent.
The colossus strode the harbor mouth in the legend.

senses.head: Walk with long steps
body: The main sense, and it carries confidence or purpose — you do not stride aimlessly. The participle stridden is rare enough that writers often rephrase to avoid it. (шагать (широким шагом), вышагивать)
examples: He tends to stride rather than walk when he is angry.
She strode to the front of the room without a note in her hand.
The coach has stridden up and down that sideline for thirty seasons.
By then he had stridden halfway across the lobby.

senses.head: Stride over, stride across
body: With a preposition it describes covering ground or stepping over an obstacle in one long step. (перешагнуть, шагать через)
examples: Long-legged birds stride across the mudflats at low tide.
He strode over the fallen branch without breaking pace.
The hikers had stridden across three fields before noon.

senses.head: Stand astride, dominate
body: Literary and now rare: to stand with a leg on either side of something, or figuratively to dominate it. Modern writing usually chooses bestride or straddle here instead. (стоять расставив ноги; возвышаться над)
examples: In the old cartoons the magnate seems to stride the whole continent.
The colossus strode the harbor mouth in the legend.

entries.register: neutral — common in narrative writing; the participle stridden is rare enough that writers rephrase
entries.contrast: The past strode is common and safe; the participle stridden is rare and sounds stiff, so most Americans recast the sentence (he had walked in) rather than say he had stridden in. Never strided.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, a verb of manner of walking; it carries purpose, so you do not stride aimlessly.
entries.transitivity: intransitive in the living senses, usually with a direction or a preposition — she strode to the front of the room, he strode over the fallen branch. The rare literary sense 3 takes an object: the colossus strode the harbor mouth.
entries.passive: no in the ordinary walking senses — ✗ the lobby had been stridden across. Even the transitive sense 3 resists it, and writers rephrase around the stiff participle stridden.

entries.meaning: To make great and sustained effort toward something difficult.
examples: Small clinics strive to keep costs down without cutting hours.
She strove for accuracy even when nobody was checking.
He has striven for that title since he was a teenager.
They had striven for years to keep the mill open.
Reformers had to strive against a century of habit.
The two houses strove with each other for a generation.
The settlers had striven against that river every spring.

senses.head: Make a great effort, aim at
body: Formal, used with to plus a verb or with for plus a goal. It implies long effort against difficulty, so it does not fit small everyday tasks. Both strove and the regular strived are accepted in American English; strove sounds more literary. (стремиться, стараться изо всех сил)
examples: Small clinics strive to keep costs down without cutting hours.
She strove for accuracy even when nobody was checking.
He has striven for that title since he was a teenager.
They had striven for years to keep the mill open.

senses.head: Contend, struggle against
body: Older and more literary: to fight or compete with someone, usually with against or with. Rare in modern speech. (бороться, состязаться (с кем-л., против чего-л.))
examples: Reformers had to strive against a century of habit.
The two houses strove with each other for a generation.
The settlers had striven against that river every spring.

entries.register: neutral to formal — mission statements and edited prose; speech says try hard
entries.contrast: American English accepts both strove/striven and the regular strived/strived. In edited prose strove is still the more common past, while strived is gaining ground as the participle. Strive takes to, for, or against, never a plain object.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, of sustained effort over time.
entries.transitivity: intransitive — it takes to plus a verb, for plus a goal, or against plus an obstacle, never a plain object: ✗ she strove accuracy; say she strove for accuracy.
entries.passive: no — intransitive, so there is nothing to promote: ✗ accuracy was striven for by her is at best stilted. Keep the active.

entries.meaning: To get hold of something, carry it, accept it, require it, or use it — the widest-ranging verb in this group.
examples: Take a napkin from the pile by the door.
She took the keys off the hook and left.
Someone has taken my umbrella from the stand.
By then the thieves had taken everything but the furniture.
I take the kids to school on my way in.
He took the package to the post office.
The neighbors have taken our mail inside all week.
It takes about twenty minutes to get downtown.
The repair took longer than the estimate said.
It has taken three years to get the permits.
Most food trucks here take cards now.
She took the job in Seattle after all.
He has never taken advice from anyone.
Take two of these with food.
He took his medication late and slept badly.
She has taken the same prescription for years.
I take the express bus when the weather is bad.
We took the coast road instead of the interstate.
They have taken that same flight every Monday.
Freshmen take two writing courses their first year.
She took organic chemistry in the summer session.
He has taken the bar exam twice.
Let's take a break before the next session.
He took a picture of the whole crew on the last day.
She has taken careful notes at every meeting.
Please do not take this the wrong way.
They took his silence as agreement.
I had taken her question for a joke until I saw her face.
Please take off your shoes at the door.
The flight took off forty minutes late.
Sales have taken off since the review came out.
The younger boy takes after his mother's side.
She took after her grandfather in temperament more than in looks.
None of the kids have taken after him in music.
A larger firm will take over the accounts in the fall.
She took on two new clients this month.
He took up the guitar at forty.
The reorganization has taken up most of the quarter.

senses.head: Get hold of, pick up
body: The base physical sense: your hand closes on something. It also covers taking what is not yours, which is why take borders on steal. (брать, взять)
examples: Take a napkin from the pile by the door.
She took the keys off the hook and left.
Someone has taken my umbrella from the stand.
By then the thieves had taken everything but the furniture.

senses.head: Carry or bring somewhere
body: Movement away from where the speaker is — you take things there and bring them here. The direction is what separates the two verbs. (относить, отвозить, брать с собой)
examples: I take the kids to school on my way in.
He took the package to the post office.
The neighbors have taken our mail inside all week.

senses.head: Require (time, effort, qualities)
body: Very common with time — it takes an hour — and with abstract requirements: it takes patience, it takes two. The subject is usually the empty it. (требовать, занимать (время, силы))
examples: It takes about twenty minutes to get downtown.
The repair took longer than the estimate said.
It has taken three years to get the permits.

senses.head: Accept, receive
body: Used of jobs, offers, advice, payment, and criticism. We take cards is the standard sign in an American store. (принимать (предложение, работу, оплату))
examples: Most food trucks here take cards now.
She took the job in Seattle after all.
He has never taken advice from anyone.

senses.head: Consume (medicine, food, drink)
body: Standard with pills and doses, and with drugs in the negative sense. With food and drink it is a little formal — take a little soup. (принимать (лекарство), употреблять)
examples: Take two of these with food.
He took his medication late and slept badly.
She has taken the same prescription for years.

senses.head: Travel by, use a route
body: You take a bus, a cab, a flight, a highway, or the next exit. It covers both the vehicle and the road. (ехать на (транспорте), сворачивать на (дорогу))
examples: I take the express bus when the weather is bad.
We took the coast road instead of the interstate.
They have taken that same flight every Monday.

senses.head: Study a subject; sit an exam
body: American academic use: you take a class and take a test. British English says sit an exam and do a course. (изучать (предмет); сдавать (экзамен))
examples: Freshmen take two writing courses their first year.
She took organic chemistry in the summer session.
He has taken the bar exam twice.

senses.head: Light-verb uses: take a break
body: Take combines with many action nouns to name the action itself: take a look, a walk, a shower, a break, a picture, a nap, notes, a seat. The meaning lives in the noun, not the verb. (делать (снимок), сделать (перерыв), взглянуть)
examples: Let's take a break before the next session.
He took a picture of the whole crew on the last day.
She has taken careful notes at every meeting.

senses.head: Regard, interpret
body: Usually with as or in fixed frames: take it as a compliment, take her seriously, take it that. It is about how you read something, not about handling it. (воспринимать, расценивать)
examples: Please do not take this the wrong way.
They took his silence as agreement.
I had taken her question for a joke until I saw her face.

senses.head: Take off
body: Four common senses on one phrasal verb: remove clothing, leave the ground, leave abruptly (informal), and suddenly succeed. Context separates them easily. (снимать (одежду); взлетать; уходить; резко пойти вверх)
examples: Please take off your shoes at the door.
The flight took off forty minutes late.
Sales have taken off since the review came out.

senses.head: Take after — resemble a relative
body: Only about family, and about looks or character rather than behavior in a single moment. Never used of things. (быть похожим на (родственника))
examples: The younger boy takes after his mother's side.
She took after her grandfather in temperament more than in looks.
None of the kids have taken after him in music.

senses.head: Take over, take on, take up
body: Three high-frequency phrasal verbs: take over means assume control of something someone else ran; take on means accept a task or hire someone; take up means start a hobby or occupy space or time. (брать на себя, перенимать; нанимать; заняться (чем-л.))
examples: A larger firm will take over the accounts in the fall.
She took on two new clients this month.
He took up the guitar at forty.
The reorganization has taken up most of the quarter.

entries.register: everyday — one of the verbs an American uses without thinking
entries.contrast: Not I have took it — the participle is taken. Keep take (away from the speaker) apart from bring (toward the speaker): take this to the office, bring me the file. Six other verbs in this group are built on it.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic across its whole range, including the light-verb uses (take a look, take a break) where the meaning sits in the noun.
entries.transitivity: transitive in nearly every sense, and the object is obligatory — ✗ she took alone. Ditransitive in the carrying sense (I take the kids their lunch), and it takes an object plus a complement in they took his silence as agreement.
