entries.passive: yes — my umbrella has been taken from the stand, the accounts will be taken over in the fall. The requirement sense resists it: ✗ twenty minutes is taken to get downtown.
entries.phrasal verbs: take aback · take after · take apart · take aside · take away · take back · take care of · take down · take for · take in · take off · take on · take out · take out on · take over · take precedence over · take to · take up · take up on · take up with
entries.see also: mistake, undertake, overtake, partake, retake, forsake, shake

entries.meaning: To drive a vehicle before buying it, or, loosely, to try anything out before committing to it.
examples: You should test-drive it on the highway, not just around the lot.
We test-drove three hybrids on Saturday.
That model has been test-driven by half the neighborhood.
By closing time he had test-driven everything on the lot.
Let's test-drive the new scheduling tool for a week.
She test-drove the joke on her sister before the toast.
The team has test-driven two different workflows this month.

senses.head: Drive a car before buying
body: The literal sense, from car sales. Written with a hyphen and inflected on the second element: test-drove, test-driven. (совершить пробную поездку, тест-драйв)
examples: You should test-drive it on the highway, not just around the lot.
We test-drove three hybrids on Saturday.
That model has been test-driven by half the neighborhood.
By closing time he had test-driven everything on the lot.

senses.head: Try something out
body: Figurative and informal, used of software, ideas, arguments, or anything you sample before adopting it. (опробовать, обкатать (что-л.))
examples: Let's test-drive the new scheduling tool for a week.
She test-drove the joke on her sister before the toast.
The team has test-driven two different workflows this month.

entries.forms: test-drive /ˈtɛst ˌdraɪv/ · test-drove /ˈtɛst ˌdroʊv/ · test-driven /ˈtɛst ˌdrɪvən/
entries.register: everyday — ordinary at a car lot, and loosely for trying anything out
entries.contrast: Built on drive and inflected exactly like it. American style hyphenates the verb but usually leaves the noun open: we took it for a test drive. It is also used loosely for trying out software, a process, or an idea.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, a verb of trying out.
entries.transitivity: transitive, and the object is obligatory — we test-drove three hybrids, let's test-drive the new scheduling tool.
entries.passive: yes — that model has been test-driven by half the neighborhood, two workflows have been test-driven this month.

entries.meaning: To grow strongly and do well — of people, businesses, plants, and animals.
examples: Small bookstores thrive in this part of the city.
The shop throve for twenty years under her father.
The cooperative has thriven despite two recessions.
By the war's end the port had thriven beyond anyone's expectation.
Basil thrives in a sunny window.
The transplanted seedlings throve after the first rain.
Nothing has thriven in that shady corner of the yard.
Some traders genuinely thrive on that kind of pressure.
She throve on deadlines her whole career.
He has thriven on being underestimated.

senses.head: Flourish, do well
body: Used of businesses, communities, and people. In American English the past is far more often the regular thrived; throve and thriven are older strong forms that survive mainly in literary writing. (процветать, преуспевать)
examples: Small bookstores thrive in this part of the city.
The shop throve for twenty years under her father.
The cooperative has thriven despite two recessions.
By the war's end the port had thriven beyond anyone's expectation.

senses.head: Grow vigorously (plants, animals)
body: The biological sense: healthy growth in good conditions. The medical phrase failure to thrive describes an infant who is not gaining weight normally. (хорошо расти, идти в рост)
examples: Basil thrives in a sunny window.
The transplanted seedlings throve after the first rain.
Nothing has thriven in that shady corner of the yard.

senses.head: Thrive on — need and enjoy
body: A fixed pattern: a person does well precisely because of something others would find hard — pressure, chaos, attention. (обожать, отлично себя чувствовать в (условиях))
examples: Some traders genuinely thrive on that kind of pressure.
She throve on deadlines her whole career.
He has thriven on being underestimated.

entries.register: everyday — the verb is common; the strong throve/thriven are literary, and Americans say thrived
entries.contrast: American English now prefers the regular thrived, thrived; the strong throve and thriven shown here are older and sound literary. Both are correct, but thrived is the safer default in edited prose. Thrive on something means to do well because of it.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in that it describes ongoing flourishing rather than a fixed state, and it takes the progressive freely: the shop is thriving.
entries.transitivity: intransitive — the thing you flourish because of follows on: she thrived on deadlines. ✗ he thrives pressure.
entries.passive: no — intransitive, so no passive exists: ✗ deadlines were thriven on by her. Only the active she thrived on deadlines.

entries.meaning: To send something through the air from your hand, and, figuratively, to put, host, or unsettle.
examples: Kids throw rocks into that creek all summer.
He threw the ball over the catcher's head.
She has thrown out the first pitch twice.
Someone had thrown a brick through the front window.
Just throw your bags in the back seat.
The judge threw him in jail for the weekend.
She has thrown herself into the campaign since January.
They throw a block party every Fourth of July.
We threw her a surprise dinner for her fiftieth.
The department has thrown a going-away party for everyone who leaves.
A question like that can throw even a prepared witness.
The change of venue threw the whole team.
Nothing in the interview had thrown her until that point.
The motion of the boat makes some passengers throw up.
He threw up twice on the drive home.
She has thrown up every morning this week.
Please do not throw away the packing slip.
He threw out every box in the garage.
The judge has thrown out the entire complaint.
A hot shower helps me throw off a headache.
The false trail threw off the search party for a day.
He has finally thrown off the flu.
The dealer will usually throw in floor mats.
They threw in a second charger with the phone.
After the third rejection he had thrown in the towel.

senses.head: Send through the air
body: The core sense, from a ball to a stone to a punch. In baseball the pitcher throws; in football the quarterback throws the ball. (бросать, кидать, метать)
examples: Kids throw rocks into that creek all summer.
He threw the ball over the catcher's head.
She has thrown out the first pitch twice.
Someone had thrown a brick through the front window.

senses.head: Put or move roughly, thrust
body: Sudden or careless placement, literal or figurative: throw your coat on the bed, throw him in jail, throw yourself into the work. (швырять, бросать (резко помещать))
examples: Just throw your bags in the back seat.
The judge threw him in jail for the weekend.
She has thrown herself into the campaign since January.

senses.head: Host an event
body: Informal but completely standard American usage, mostly with party: throw a party, throw a shower, throw someone a birthday dinner. (устраивать (вечеринку, приём))
examples: They throw a block party every Fourth of July.
We threw her a surprise dinner for her fiftieth.
The department has thrown a going-away party for everyone who leaves.

senses.head: Confuse, unsettle
body: Informal: an unexpected question or event throws a person. The object is a person, and it turns up most often in the past — that threw me. (сбивать с толку, выбивать из колеи)
examples: A question like that can throw even a prepared witness.
The change of venue threw the whole team.
Nothing in the interview had thrown her until that point.

senses.head: Throw up — vomit
body: The ordinary everyday word for vomiting in American English; vomit itself sounds clinical. Throw up can also mean to build hastily, but the illness sense dominates. (тошнить, рвать)
examples: The motion of the boat makes some passengers throw up.
He threw up twice on the drive home.
She has thrown up every morning this week.

senses.head: Throw away, throw out — discard
body: Literal for trash and figurative for wasted chances: throw away an opportunity. Throw out also means to eject a person or to reject a case. (выбрасывать; упускать (шанс))
examples: Please do not throw away the packing slip.
He threw out every box in the garage.
The judge has thrown out the entire complaint.

senses.head: Throw off — shed; mislead
body: To get rid of something clinging — an illness, a mood, a pursuer — or to send someone in the wrong direction. (сбросить (с себя); сбить со следа)
examples: A hot shower helps me throw off a headache.
The false trail threw off the search party for a day.
He has finally thrown off the flu.

senses.head: Throw in — add for free
body: A seller throws in an extra at no charge; separately, throw in the towel is a fixed idiom from boxing meaning to quit. (добавить в придачу; сдаться (throw in the towel))
examples: The dealer will usually throw in floor mats.
They threw in a second charger with the phone.
After the third rejection he had thrown in the towel.

entries.register: everyday — one of the verbs an American uses without thinking
entries.contrast: The past threw /θru/ is a homophone of through, and the participle thrown sounds like throne. Not I have threw it away — use I have thrown it away.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in every sense, from a pitch to hosting a party to unsettling a witness.
entries.transitivity: transitive in most senses (he threw the ball, they throw a block party, the change of venue threw the team), ditransitive in we threw her a surprise dinner, and intransitive in he threw up twice.
entries.passive: yes — the entire complaint has been thrown out, a brick had been thrown through the window. The idiom throw up has no passive: ✗ lunch was thrown up.
entries.phrasal verbs: throw away · throw back · throw in · throw off · throw on · throw out · throw over · throw together · throw up

entries.meaning: To offer a lower price than a competitor, or, in card games, to bid below the true strength of your hand.
examples: Two firms tried to underbid us on the same contract.
The smaller shop underbade everyone and then could not finish the work.
We have been underbidden on every municipal job this year.
By the deadline they had underbidden the incumbent by nearly a third.
Cautious partners underbid good hands out of habit.
She underbade a hand worth an easy game.
He has underbidden twice tonight and it cost us the rubber.

senses.head: Bid lower than a rival
body: Commercial: contractors underbid each other to win work. Note that in ordinary American business English the past and participle are simply underbid; the strong forms underbade and underbidden listed for this entry follow bid — bade — bidden and are archaic. (предложить более низкую цену, сбить цену)
examples: Two firms tried to underbid us on the same contract.
The smaller shop underbade everyone and then could not finish the work.
We have been underbidden on every municipal job this year.
By the deadline they had underbidden the incumbent by nearly a third.

senses.head: Bid below your hand (cards)
body: In bridge, to make a contract lower than your cards justify, giving away points you could have earned. Technical to card play. (заявить меньше, чем позволяет карта (в бридже))
examples: Cautious partners underbid good hands out of habit.
She underbade a hand worth an easy game.
He has underbidden twice tonight and it cost us the rubber.

entries.register: rare — contracting and card play; underbade/underbidden are archaic
entries.contrast: In American business English underbid is normally invariable — underbid, underbid, underbid — because it inherits the auction sense of bid. The forms underbade and underbidden given here come from the old command sense and sound wrong in a sentence about contracts; use underbid for both past and participle.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, a verb of bidding.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive with a rival or a hand as the object (two firms tried to underbid us, she underbade a hand worth an easy game), intransitive in cautious partners underbid out of habit.
entries.passive: yes — we have been underbidden on every municipal job this year, though ordinary American business English would say we were underbid.

entries.meaning: To lie beneath something, either physically or as its hidden basis or cause.
examples: Two assumptions underlie the entire proposal.
Old resentments underlay the whole dispute.
A simple idea has underlain the company's strategy from the start.
Fear of another shortage had underlain every decision that year.
Limestone beds underlie most of the county.
A layer of peat underlay the topsoil.
Solid granite has underlain the site all along.

senses.head: Be the basis or cause of
body: The common sense, and it is abstract: an assumption, a principle, or a tension underlies an argument, a policy, or a conflict. Often met as the adjective underlying. (лежать в основе, быть подоплёкой)
examples: Two assumptions underlie the entire proposal.
Old resentments underlay the whole dispute.
A simple idea has underlain the company's strategy from the start.
Fear of another shortage had underlain every decision that year.

senses.head: Lie physically underneath
body: The literal geological or structural sense — one layer sits below another. Compare overlie, which is its exact mirror. (залегать под, находиться внизу)
examples: Limestone beds underlie most of the county.
A layer of peat underlay the topsoil.
Solid granite has underlain the site all along.

entries.register: formal — academic and technical writing; the adjective underlying is far more common
entries.third person: underlies · -ing form: underlying (the ie becomes y)
entries.contrast: Built on lie and inflected exactly like it. The past underlay is spelled like the noun an underlay (the padding beneath a carpet), and by far the commonest form in American writing is the adjective underlying: the underlying cause.
entries.verb type: stative — it names a relation of one thing to another, not an event, and it stays out of the progressive: ✗ two assumptions are underlying the proposal; say two assumptions underlie the proposal.
entries.transitivity: transitive, unlike its base verb lie — old resentments underlay the whole dispute, limestone beds underlie most of the county.
entries.passive: restricted — standard and common in the geological sense (the site is underlain by solid granite), stiff in the abstract one, where writers reach for the adjective instead: the underlying cause.

entries.meaning: To take on a task or responsibility, or to give a formal promise to do something.
examples: The agency will undertake a full review of the program.
They undertook the restoration without any public money.
The lab has undertaken three studies on the same question.
By spring the team had undertaken the largest survey in its history.
The seller undertakes to deliver within thirty days.
He undertook to repay the loan in full by June.
The city has undertaken to maintain the trail in perpetuity.
The same firm undertook for most of the county in the 1890s.
His family had undertaken for three generations in that town.

senses.head: Take on, begin (a task)
body: Formal, with a substantial object: a study, a project, a journey, a review. You do not undertake small errands. (предпринимать, браться за)
examples: The agency will undertake a full review of the program.
They undertook the restoration without any public money.
The lab has undertaken three studies on the same question.
By spring the team had undertaken the largest survey in its history.

senses.head: Formally promise, commit
body: Legal and contractual, with to plus a verb: a party undertakes to deliver, pay, or maintain. The noun an undertaking names the promise itself. (обязываться, брать на себя обязательство)
examples: The seller undertakes to deliver within thirty days.
He undertook to repay the loan in full by June.
The city has undertaken to maintain the trail in perpetuity.

senses.head: Arrange funerals
body: The source of the noun undertaker, but the verb in this sense is now dated and rare; today one says work as a funeral director. (заниматься похоронным делом)
examples: The same firm undertook for most of the county in the 1890s.
His family had undertaken for three generations in that town.

entries.register: neutral to formal — business, legal, and academic writing
entries.contrast: Built on take and inflected exactly like it. Undertake to do something means to promise to do it. The noun undertaker, a funeral director, comes from an old sense of the verb, and an undertaking is a project or a formal promise.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, of taking on a task or making a commitment.
entries.transitivity: transitive with a substantial object (the agency will undertake a full review), or with to plus a verb in the promising sense (he undertook to repay the loan). The archaic funeral sense is intransitive: the same firm undertook for most of the county.
entries.passive: yes — three studies have been undertaken on the same question, the largest survey in its history had been undertaken by spring.

entries.meaning: To accept financial risk for something — an insurance policy, a securities issue — or, more broadly, to pay for it.
examples: Few insurers will underwrite coastal property at that elevation now.
Lloyd's syndicates underwrote the voyage for a hefty premium.
The carrier has underwritten this fleet for a decade.
Nobody had underwritten a rig that far offshore before.
Two banks will underwrite the offering.
The firm underwrote the largest IPO of the year.
That syndicate has underwritten most of the state's bond issues.
A local foundation will underwrite the summer concerts.
Her employer underwrote the whole conference.
Listeners have underwritten this station since 1974.

senses.head: Assume insurance risk
body: The original sense, from insurers signing their names under a policy. An underwriter decides whether the risk is acceptable and at what price. (страховать, принимать риск на страхование)
examples: Few insurers will underwrite coastal property at that elevation now.
Lloyd's syndicates underwrote the voyage for a hefty premium.
The carrier has underwritten this fleet for a decade.
Nobody had underwritten a rig that far offshore before.

senses.head: Guarantee a securities issue
body: Investment banking: a bank buys or guarantees an entire issue of stock or bonds and resells it, absorbing the risk that it does not sell. (гарантировать размещение (ценных бумаг))
examples: Two banks will underwrite the offering.
The firm underwrote the largest IPO of the year.
That syndicate has underwritten most of the state's bond issues.

senses.head: Fund, sponsor
body: General and now very common, especially of foundations and public broadcasting: to pay for something and absorb any loss. (финансировать, спонсировать)
examples: A local foundation will underwrite the summer concerts.
Her employer underwrote the whole conference.
Listeners have underwritten this station since 1974.

entries.register: formal — insurance and finance; a technical term
entries.third person: underwrites · -ing form: underwriting (drop the e; keep both r's)
entries.contrast: Built on write and inflected exactly like it, but the stress differs from its cousins: underwrite is usually UN-der-ryte, matching the noun underwriter, while rewrite as a verb takes the stress on the second part.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, a verb of assuming risk or paying for something.
entries.transitivity: transitive, and the object is obligatory — a policy, an issue, or an event: two banks will underwrite the offering.
entries.passive: yes, and it is the natural form in finance — the offering was underwritten by two banks, this station has been underwritten by listeners since 1974.

entries.meaning: To unfasten something, to reverse an action, or, in older language, to ruin someone.
examples: I cannot undo this knot with cold hands.
He undid the top button and loosened his tie.
Someone has undone the latch on the gate.
By the time we found the crate, the twine had been undone.
You can undo the last five edits with the arrow.
That single email undid six months of goodwill.
The new agreement has undone most of the damage.
Nothing had undone the harm of the first announcement.
Vanity will undo a careful negotiator faster than bad luck.
His own memos undid him at the hearing.
The family had been undone by a single bad harvest.
My shoelace comes undone every mile or so.
The whole schedule came undone after the second delay.
He had come undone well before the trial ended.

senses.head: Unfasten, untie, open
body: The literal sense — buttons, laces, knots, zippers, packages. The opposite of do up. (развязывать, расстёгивать, отвинчивать)
examples: I cannot undo this knot with cold hands.
He undid the top button and loosened his tie.
Someone has undone the latch on the gate.
By the time we found the crate, the twine had been undone.

senses.head: Reverse an action
body: Figurative and, since computers, everywhere: undo the last change, Ctrl+Z. Often in the pattern cannot be undone, meaning permanent. (отменить, вернуть назад (действие))
examples: You can undo the last five edits with the arrow.
That single email undid six months of goodwill.
The new agreement has undone most of the damage.
Nothing had undone the harm of the first announcement.

senses.head: Ruin, destroy (a person)
body: Formal and literary, and often passive: he was undone by his own pride. The old fixed cry I am undone means ruined. (погубить, разорить)
examples: Vanity will undo a careful negotiator faster than bad luck.
His own memos undid him at the hearing.
The family had been undone by a single bad harvest.

senses.head: Come undone
body: A fixed phrase with come: literally a knot or seam comes loose, figuratively a plan or a person falls apart. (развязаться, разладиться, расклеиться)
examples: My shoelace comes undone every mile or so.
The whole schedule came undone after the second delay.
He had come undone well before the trial ended.

entries.register: everyday — Ctrl+Z and undo the damage
entries.contrast: Built on do and inflected exactly like it, third person undoes included. Undone also lives on as an adjective meaning unfastened or ruined: his shoelace came undone, we are undone.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, of unfastening and of reversing. The participle undone doubles as an adjective: his shoelace came undone.
entries.transitivity: transitive, and the object is obligatory — he undid the top button, that single email undid six months of goodwill. The fixed come undone uses come, not undo.
entries.passive: yes, and the fixed negative passive is everywhere — the damage cannot be undone, someone has undone the latch, the twine had been undone.

entries.meaning: To take something back or take it out, to move back from a place, or to become distant from people.
examples: You can withdraw up to five hundred dollars a day.
She withdrew the whole balance and closed the account.
He has withdrawn money twice this week.
By Friday they had withdrawn nearly all of the deposit.
I withdraw the question, Your Honor.
The company withdrew its offer after the inspection.
Prosecutors have withdrawn two of the charges.
Two candidates withdraw from the primary every cycle.
He withdrew from the tournament with a shoulder injury.
She has withdrawn from three classes this semester.
The commander decided to withdraw the forward units.
The jury withdrew to deliberate just after four.
Peacekeepers have withdrawn from the eastern districts.
Teenagers sometimes withdraw from family entirely for a while.
He withdrew into his work after the divorce.
She has withdrawn from almost everyone she used to see.
Patients should not withdraw from this medication abruptly.
He withdrew from nicotine over about six weeks.
She has withdrawn from the sedatives under supervision.

senses.head: Take money out
body: Banking, and the first sense most learners meet. The noun is a withdrawal, and it is what an ATM performs. (снимать (деньги со счёта))
examples: You can withdraw up to five hundred dollars a day.
She withdrew the whole balance and closed the account.
He has withdrawn money twice this week.
By Friday they had withdrawn nearly all of the deposit.

senses.head: Take back, retract
body: Used of statements, offers, applications, charges, and products. Formal but common in news and business. (отзывать, брать назад (заявление, предложение))
examples: I withdraw the question, Your Honor.
The company withdrew its offer after the inspection.
Prosecutors have withdrawn two of the charges.

senses.head: Pull out of, quit
body: Intransitive with from: a candidate, a student, or a country stops taking part. (выходить (из гонки, конкурса), отказываться от участия)
examples: Two candidates withdraw from the primary every cycle.
He withdrew from the tournament with a shoulder injury.
She has withdrawn from three classes this semester.

senses.head: Retreat, move back (troops, people)
body: Both transitive (a general withdraws forces) and intransitive (troops withdraw). Also used of people leaving a room formally. (отводить (войска); отступать; удаляться)
examples: The commander decided to withdraw the forward units.
The jury withdrew to deliberate just after four.
Peacekeepers have withdrawn from the eastern districts.

senses.head: Become distant, withdrawn
body: Psychological, about a person retreating from contact. Most often met as the adjective withdrawn — a quiet, closed-off person. (замыкаться в себе, отдаляться)
examples: Teenagers sometimes withdraw from family entirely for a while.
He withdrew into his work after the divorce.
She has withdrawn from almost everyone she used to see.

senses.head: Withdraw from a drug
body: Medical: to stop taking a substance the body has come to depend on. The noun withdrawal names the symptoms that follow. (прекращать приём (вещества), проходить ломку)
examples: Patients should not withdraw from this medication abruptly.
He withdrew from nicotine over about six weeks.
She has withdrawn from the sedatives under supervision.

entries.register: everyday — money from an ATM, a name from a race
entries.contrast: Built on draw and inflected exactly like it, never withdrawed. The participle also works as an adjective for a quiet, distant person: he grew withdrawn after the move.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in every sense, including the psychological he withdrew into his work.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive with money, a statement, or troops (she withdrew the whole balance, the company withdrew its offer), intransitive with from (he withdrew from the tournament, patients should not withdraw abruptly).
entries.passive: yes in the transitive senses — two of the charges have been withdrawn, the forward units were withdrawn overnight. No passive of he withdrew from the tournament.
entries.phrasal verbs: withdraw into

entries.meaning: To form letters and words, to compose a text, and to communicate or record in writing.
examples: Kids write their names before they can read them.
He wrote the address on the back of a receipt.
She has written the same phrase on every page.
Someone had written the date in pencil in the corner.
He writes for two magazines and teaches on the side.
She wrote her first novel in a rented cabin.
They have written four reports on the same landfill.
Write me when you get settled.
She wrote to her brother every Sunday for years.
He has written to the department three times without an answer.
The clinic will write you a prescription today.
The officer wrote him a ticket for the expired tag.
Her manager has written her up twice for being late.
She writes most of the band's material.
He wrote that melody in a single afternoon.
They have written together since high school.
We write most of the tooling in Python.
The script wrote the results to a temporary file.
He has written every line of that parser himself.
Write it down before you forget the number.
The bank wrote off the remaining balance.
Critics had written him off years before his best season.

senses.head: Form letters and words
body: The physical act — pen on paper, chalk on a board. The classic learner trap sits here: not I have wrote but I have written. (писать (буквы, слова))
examples: Kids write their names before they can read them.
He wrote the address on the back of a receipt.
She has written the same phrase on every page.
Someone had written the date in pencil in the corner.

senses.head: Compose a text or work
body: The authorial sense: books, articles, reports, essays. Used intransitively, she writes can mean she is a writer by trade. (писать, сочинять (книгу, статью))
examples: He writes for two magazines and teaches on the side.
She wrote her first novel in a rented cabin.
They have written four reports on the same landfill.

senses.head: Write to someone, correspond
body: American English allows write me as well as write to me; British English keeps the to. Used of letters and email alike. (писать (кому-л.), переписываться)
examples: Write me when you get settled.
She wrote to her brother every Sunday for years.
He has written to the department three times without an answer.

senses.head: Write a check, write up
body: To fill out a formal document: a check, a prescription, a ticket, an invoice. Write up also means to prepare a report or to cite someone formally. (выписывать (чек, счёт, штраф))
examples: The clinic will write you a prescription today.
The officer wrote him a ticket for the expired tag.
Her manager has written her up twice for being late.

senses.head: Compose music
body: Standard for songs, scores, and arrangements — you write a song the way you write a poem. (писать (музыку), сочинять)
examples: She writes most of the band's material.
He wrote that melody in a single afternoon.
They have written together since high school.

senses.head: Write code; write data
body: Two technical senses: programmers write software, and a program writes data to a disk or a file. Both are everyday vocabulary in computing. (писать (код); записывать (данные))
examples: We write most of the tooling in Python.
The script wrote the results to a temporary file.
He has written every line of that parser himself.

senses.head: Write down, write off
body: Write down means to record on paper. Write off has two senses: cancel a debt or reduce an asset's book value, and dismiss a person or thing as hopeless. (записать; списать (долг); поставить крест на)
examples: Write it down before you forget the number.
The bank wrote off the remaining balance.
Critics had written him off years before his best season.

entries.register: everyday — one of the verbs an American uses without thinking
entries.third person: writes · -ing form: writing (drop the e; one t)
entries.contrast: Not I have wrote — the participle is written, with two t's, while writing has one. The w is silent throughout, so write is a homophone of right, and wrote of rote. Americans can say write me without to; British English keeps write to me.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, a verb of creation and of recording.
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive in he writes for two magazines, transitive with a text or a document (she wrote her first novel), and ditransitive in American English: the clinic will write you a prescription, write me when you get settled.
entries.passive: yes — the same phrase has been written on every page, the remaining balance was written off, she has been written up twice for being late.
entries.phrasal verbs: write back · write down · write in · write off · write out · write up
